item.title: Is Prediction Better Than Retrodiction?
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
In internet debate spheres around philosophy—and especially around philosophy of religion—people will often haggle over whether making retrodictions is as good as predictions. I.e., do predictions have evidential value when you already know what happened? And if so, do they have just as much evidential value?

I thought I might as well settle this once and for all, so that we don’t have to discuss this any more. I think the answer is pretty clear: Retrodictions are no worse in principle. Still, they are in general quite a bit worse, due to the limitations of us reasoners.

In Theory? No.

In theory, retrodictions are perfectly fine. In fact, they’re equally as good. I don’t think that there is a plausible way of giving a theoretically “deep” explanation of why predictions are better. Any approach that makes retrodiction worse as a matter of the basic theory will run into rampant absurdities!

item.title: Evolution Doesn't Solve Psychophysical Harmony
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
In the decade of our Lord, the 2020’s, philosophers and blessed the world with a new argument for theism: The argument from psychophysical harmony. The internet has not been the same since (though I don’t know how much of that is thanks to the argument).

This argument is often misunderstood. Many people immediately dismiss it as ridiculous; many people take some time, and then dismiss it as ridiculous; and then there are those who end up finding it plausible and defending it. I have at least a foot in the latter camp, and so I wanted to explain why some of the most common intuitive reactions against the argument don’t work.1

Specifically, I’ll focus on how: 1) Evolution does not dissolve the argument, and 2) the argument does not require epiphenomenalism.

The Argument from Psychophysical Harmony

The argument is easiest to explain by assuming epiphenomenalism. I know that isn’t really a good look for me, considering that my thesis is that it does not assume epiphenomenalism. Rest assured that it does, in fact, not. We will relax this assumption later—but it’s easiest to understand the other moves in the argument this way.

So, yes, let’s assume epiphenomenalism for now. Okay, now, imagine that you are some kind of superbaby behind a kind of veil of ignorance, where you have not yet seen anything about what the world is like, but are otherwise perfectly intelligent. In this position, what kind of conscious experience would you expect to be associated with any particular physical state or process or whatever?

Well, it seems like there are a lot of options! Consider the physical event that is my body touching a hot stove, and pulling its hand away—with all the associated brain processes and whatnot included. Just given the physical facts of this event, its perfectly coherent that any number of experiences might be associated with it. There could be pain—but there could also be pleasure, the feeling of lukewarm bathwater, or just complete static.

Again, if we’re assuming epiphenomenalism this is certainly true! Given our actual situation, these alternatives might seem pretty strange, but we can’t rule them out a priori. Not just that, but if we’re assuming that reality is fundamentally indifferent to value, it’s hard to see what reason we could even have to think that any particular experience be associated with any particular physical process. It seems we should just be more or less indifferent over the possible options—perhaps favoring simpler pairings. Again, at least if we’re assuming epiphenominalism.

On the other hand, suppose that God exists—God in the sense of a perfectly good (or at least very very good) being. Well, since God is good, then if he exists, we should think that something being good makes it more likely to occur, all else being equal.

Now consider the value of a “disharmonious” world—a world where the physical processes run exactly the same as in the actual world, but where our mental states have been completely scrambled, e.g. into random static, or into pain and pleasure being swapped. I can at least report that I would personally not find such a world particularly desirable! It seems to me that it’s plausibly better to have a “harmonious” world where our experiences are more or less coherent.

If that’s true then a harmonious world will be more likely on theism than on an indifference hypothesis, meaning that the world being harmonious would be evidence for theism over indifference.

Now the veil of ignorance is lifted, and—lo!—the world in fact is harmonious! By the above reasoning, this fact gives us some evidence for theism.

Evolution

The first thing everyone thinks when they hear this argument is “well it’s obvious—evolution explains the pairings.” I mean, imagine a creature whose mental life is static. Such a creature would be a babbling fool, who’d in all likelihood just lie on the ground and drool until it died. Hence disharmonious creatures would be selected away, and harmonious creatures would survive and reproduce, giving us a perfectly good explanation with no God needed. It’s just as with most things: Where there seems to be design, it’s most likely an evolutionary process.

Before proceeding, I’d like to add a caveat:

Everyone, including the proponent of the argument, agrees that evolution does explain our experiences in an important sense! Why do I feel pain and pull my hand away when I put it on a stove? Well, it’s because creatures who did not feel pain did not pull their hands away; and creatures who did not pull their hands away got nasty burns on their hands and died (perhaps a bit of an anachronistic example). So evolution obviously does explain psychophysical harmony in an important sense.

Nevertheless, I’ll be a little blunt here: If you think evolution dissolves the argument from psychophysical harmony, you have not understood what the argument is about.

Again, let me assume epiphenomenalism for now. This is still only pedagogical—hold your horses, I’ll explain why it’s not needed soon enough. In this case you can imagine the physical like a bunch of locomotives driving around on tracks, and the mental as the smoke coming out of their chimneys.

Let’s say that trains that work well get copied in new designs, and trains that don’t work well are scrapped. After a while, it turns out that all the trains that do the best have pink smoke coming out of their chimneys. In this analogy, the trains are of course the physical world, and the replication and scrapping are evolution; while the smoke is the mental.

We might then ask why the best trains have pink smoke coming out of their chimneys. By this we might mean two different things:

  1. Why, given the actual facts about fuel, engines, colors, etc. do the best trains have pink smoke?

This question is answered perfectly well by train-evolution. What we’re asking is basically just why the best trains have such-and-such fuel and engines (the ones that happen to produce pink smoke). The answer to this is that such-and-such fuel and engines are better and so they end up being the ones in the best trains. Great!

But we might also ask:

  1. Why do such-and-such fuel and engines produce pink smoke to begin with.

This question is not answered by train-evolution! After all, train evolution is not sensitive to the color of the smoke itself. Rather it is just sensitive to how good the trains on the ground are. So when “deciding” the color of the smoke, train-evolution just works with the facts about which fuels produce which color smoke in the background.

If such-and-such fuel and engines (the best ones) had instead happened to produce green smoke, then train-evolution would have run its course and given us trains that produce green smoke. So train-evolution can’t be the answer to our second question.

Furthermore, we might suppose that we had really strong prior reason to expect that God wants pink smoke to come out of locomotives (at this point the analogy may begin to strain).

The analogy should hopefully be clear enough, but let me just draw it out to make sure you get it. When we ask “why do we have harmonious mental lives?” we could be asking two questions:

  1. Why, given the actual facts about psychophysical pairings, do we have harmonious lives?

As I said in my caveat, this question is answered by evolution. This was never in doubt—everyone on all sides of the discussion already agreed, and it is not any sort of hole in the argument.

Or we might be asking:

  1. Why are the psychophysical pairings what they are to begin with?

This question cannot be answered by evolution. Evolution works with the the psychophysical pairings in the background. It can only select for a creature’s feeling pain when burnt by selecting for genes that make a creature undergo the physical process that produces pain when burnt. It can only select for this physical process—it cannot select for the fact that this physical process produces pain.

It’s just like how evolution selects for insects to have chitinous exoskeletons. It selects for this because chitin can be hard. But evolution does not select for the fact that chitin can be hard. That is a fact that results from more fundamental physics and chemistry, and evolution just has to work with that in the background.

I’ll explain why epiphenomenalism is not needed in a second. But I just want to underline that everyone should agree that this second question cannot be answered by evolution, no matter what you think about the rest of the argument:

  1. Epiphenomenalists should not, as should be clear by now.

  2. Interactionist dualists should not, because evolution just works with the facts about which physical states cause which mental states and vice versa in the background.2

  3. Type B physicalists should not, because what mental state corresponds to what physical state is a necessary fact. And evolution is not in the business of changing necessary facts.

  4. Type A physicalists should not, because there was not any question as to what the “psychophysical pairings” were gonna be in the first place. Evolution is not needed to explain anything.3

So as I said, no matter which way you slice it, invoking evolution is simply not a good objection to the argument from psychophysical harmony. Whether or not you think the argument is a total disaster—whether or not it’s the most ridiculous thing you’ve ever heard—you should at least be able to understand that evolution is not an answer to the argument except in a trivial sense that even proponents agree to. If you do not understand this, you have not understood what the argument is about.

No Epiphenomenalism Needed

Okay, so I’ve been laying out everything so far under the supposition of epiphenomenalism. You may rightly think that this is slightly strange, seeing as my thesis is that epiphenomenalism is not required for the argument. Well, the long-promised section in which I explain how to do the argument without epiphenomenalism has finally arrived.

Let’s start from the view closest to epiphenomenalism and work our way towards the most distinct views.

Interactionist Dualism

What happens if we stick with dualism, but relax the assumption that mental states have no effect on the physical? The thing to see is that just because there is a causal relation, it is not given that this will be a harmonious one.

Consider an analogy:

I have a camera and a TV. On the TV I see a nice forest landscape.

From the TV I see a wire going to a camera, and the camera is pointing at a piece of paper. I cannot see what is on the paper. But i notice that if I push the paper to the right, the image of the screen is also offset to the right; when I tilt the paper, the image on the screen appears to tilt; and so on.

From this I may of course infer that the piece of paper simply contains an image of the same scene I see on the TV, and the image on the TV is caused by the picture.

But here is an alternate hypothesis. It might be that the paper looks like this:

Then it would still be true that the image on the screen is caused by the paper—the camera would simply be inverting the image and displaying it on the screen.

It could also be that the paper is simply blank, except for a single dot. Then the camera is tracking the dot, and is itself providing the rest of the information of the image, yet what we see on the screen is still caused by the paper. Et cetera, et cetera.

The point of this analogy is that simply adding in the supposition that A is caused by B does not automatically tell us what B is like.

In the camera example, we would probably infer that the image on the paper is like that on the screen, given what we know about cameras and screens. But if the rest of the psychophysical harmony argument is to be trusted, then merely adding in the supposition that our behavior is caused by our mental states does not ensure a priori that we get harmonious pairings.

Even if my pulling my hand away from the stove is caused by my experiences, it’s not given that the experience that causes that behavior is pain. And if we don’t have very strong reason to expect that certain causal connections are much more likely a priori than others, given an indifference hypothesis, then the argument still runs as before.

Now, if you think that the relevant causal connections are a priori necessary, this is no longer true (see footnote 2).

Russellian Monism

This is even more straightforward. On russellian monism, our behavior is caused by our mental states, since our brain states just are our mental states. Our phenomenal consciousness is merely quiddities that play the role of our mental states—and typically russellian monists think that it’s possible for the quiddities to be different but the physical properties to be the same (e.g. for there to be philosophical zombies).

If this is right, then it’s true that our behavior is caused by our mental states. But those mental states could have been different, yet our behavior the same, and so everything about the argument runs through the same.

Type B Physicalism

Type B physicalism is the big one, where it’s most surprising that the argument might still work. After all, on physicalism, the psychophysical pairings are metaphysically necessary. So it might seem sort of strange to wonder about how lucky it is that we got these pairings, when it couldn’t have gone any other way.

Yet, this doesn’t escape the argument. We can see this by help of a few analogies:

You suddenly hear a booming trumpet sound. Surprised, you go to your window and look up to see rows of angels descending from heaven, singing songs declaring the glory of God. Text appears before your eyes, seemingly floating in mid air:

“Rejoice, all of creation, for the LORD your God has returned!”

Up on some clouds, a set of pearly gates appear, and you begin floating—phasing through your roof and everything—towards the gates. Looking around you, you see all the people of the earth similarly floating up towards the heavens.

To your great surprise you look to your right only to see Baruch Spinoza in the flesh, within talking distance. You say to him:

“This is incredible! It seems that God does exist after all!”

Oddly calm in his demeanor, he replies:

“Eh, I don’t think so. Maybe God-or-Nature, but not some kind of theistic God.”

“What do you mean?! Don’t you see what is happening?? This is incredible vindication of theism!”

“Not really. I believe that everything that happens is necessary. So this isn’t actually a surprising turn of events—this had to happen, so there’s no point in being all surprised that it did.”

Spinoza’s response here is irrational—I hope we can agree on that much.4 But this shows that the mere fact that something is necessary does not show that it is unsurprising.

More specifically, the problem seems to be this: The theory that some fact is necessary does not automatically tell you what particular thing is necessary. Simply being a physicalist doesn’t tell us what the psychophysical pairings will be, and so it can still be very surprising that they turn out to be what they are.

However, even if this is right, you might still worry that God is not much of a help here. I mean, the psychophysical pairing is still necessary, and so even if it’s surprising, it’s not like God could be the reason why it is what it is—unless we think that God can do the impossible.

Here we start to stray from the austere promise that psychophysical harmony doesn’t conflict with anything other than type A physicalism. Because it might turn out that we have to abandon physicalism in the end. The other analogies have been quite close to Crummett and Cutter’s, but here I’ll just directly lift an analogy from the original paper (pp. 35-36):

You’re about to visit the island of boulders. You don’t know whether anyone has been there before. You’re fairly (but not extremely) confident that boulders are not humanly moveable, so even if there were previous visitors, they couldn’t have controlled the arrangement of boulders on the island. (Boulders are very heavy, after all.) When you arrive at the island, you observe the boulders arranged in a nice circular pattern, like Stonehenge.

In this case, it seems that you should conclude that the boulders have been arranged by humans, even though you thought that this was impossible.

Analogously, if you’re a type B physicalist, you should agree that psychophysical harmony is striking and surprising. But given physicalism, theism isn’t much help. So it seems like you should do the analogous thing to the boulder case: You should move towards the view that the psychophysical pairings are not necessary, and that they were designed (assuming the rest of the argument is sound)—so long as you’re not extremely certain about physicalism in advance.

So it may be that in the end accepting the argument requires giving up physicalism. Still, the argument does not presume physicalism. It just presumes that the psychophysical pairings are not a priori necessary, and then it may turn out to be evidence for non-physicalism+God.

Notice for all of these, that we have allowed your mental states to cause your behavior, and yet this doesn’t automatically solve the problem of psychophysical harmony—and importantly, evolution still doesn’t provide a solution to the problem.

After all, what psychophysical harmony points to is the surprisingness of which mental states cause which physical states or vice versa—or which physical states/processes are which mental states.

E.g. suppose you’re a type B identity theorist. For all you know a priori, the brains state (call it brain state B) that causes you to avoid something could be pain, or pleasure, or whatever else. Evolution explains why brain state B occurs when you burn your hand—but it doesn’t explain why brain state B is pain. For all you know, brain state B could have turned out to be pleasure, and so there’s still a problem of psychophysical harmony, even after evolution has done its thing.

And notice that either way, it’s still your mental state that causes your avoidance. If brain state B turns out to be pain, your pain is the thing that causes your avoidance; and if B turns out to be pleasure, your pleasure will be the thing that causes your avoidance.

You may still think: “Okay, sure, this is technically not epiphenomenalism, but it’s still awfully close in effect. If you can just swap around mental states willy nilly without changing anything, that’s epiphenomenalism in effect.”

This is, however, wrongheaded! Even if there are pairs of possible worlds that are physically the same, but with different mental states, that does not mean that your mental states don’t cause your behavior.

I could similarly say: “Oh so you think that there are two possible worlds, both of which have me die—but in the one I’m killed by a bullet, and the other I’m killed by a sword? That’s just epiphenomenalism in disguise!”

That’d of course be ridiculous. Perhaps I’m killed by a bullet in the actual world. In that case my death is caused by the bullet—had I not been hit, I’d not have died. Still there is another possible world where I’m killed by a sword. In both of these worlds, my death is caused by the thing in question, even though it’s possible for it to be caused by something else. There’s no trickery involved!

Type A Physicalism

There is a way of escaping the argument, which is by being a type A physicalist. In this case you think that the psychophysical “pairings” are a priori necessary. That is, it’s not ideally conceivable that you could have the brain state associated with pain, without being in pain.

On this view, the problem straightforwardly vanishes. It’s no more surprising or mysterious that we have the psychophysical pairings we do than that (√2)2 happens to be 2. At least in principle—obviously it’s very complicated and difficult to figure out what someone is experiencing from what’s going on in their head in practice.

Similarly, you might hold something that’s on the border between type A and type B physicalism. Perhaps you think that zombies are conceivable, but you think that if something is conscious it's inconceivable that it feeling pain doesn't dispose you to avoid the pain. If you hold this for all the relevant cases of purported harmony, then you may also be off the hook, even if you aren't strictly a type A physicalist.

What Do I Make of the Argument?

From this post you might gather that I’m very confident that the argument from psychophysical harmony works. That’s not true, however. I’m pretty confident that it works as an argument for the disjunction of type A physicalism and theism. But unlike most of the people who present this argument, I’m not super confident that type A physicalism is incorrect.

I still lean towards the argument working, since I lean against type A physicalism. But I can sympathize with the people who are suspicious of the PH argument. Just intuitively for me, it doesn’t pass the sniff test very well. With fine-tuning or something, it’s at least intuitively compelling evidence for theism. But psychophysical harmony is such an “academic” problem that it’s just hard for me to be compelled at an intuitive level.

That doesn’t automatically mean it’s wrong. If there’s a mismatch between how I assess an argument on the merits, and how compelling it seems from an intuitive outside perspective, it can go two ways. Perhaps I’m just intuitively underestimating the problem because psychophysical harmony is such an unobvious problem;5 or perhaps I’m getting lost in the intricate frameworks needed to make the argument work, and I should trust my gut. I’m not sure which is right here.

If you also think that the argument from psychophysical harmony just seems a little suspicious on its face, that’s perfectly fine. I think it’s rational enough to side agaisnt an argument if you’re not sure where it goes wrong, and you’re not willing to spend the effort to understand it in depth. But if you choose to do so, I would advise you against calling the argument ridiculous and crazy, and assuming that proponents of it are confused fools, when you yourself have evidently not understood what it is even about.

This button exhibits clickysubscribal harmony:

1

This is partly as a result of the response I got to a recent Note.

2

Actually, an important caveat: If you think that the causal powers of mental states are a priori, then there might actually be an exception here. After all, this would mean that it’d be a priori inconsistent for pain to cause any other reaction than it does. If this is right, then we simply couldn’t conceivably have had disharmony, given evolution.

However, this would be a sort of strange position, since dualism tends to be motivated by certain considerations about conceivability—and it would be strange if the causality in the other direction were a priori.

3

A similar thing could be said for type C physicalism.

4

To be clear, Spinoza’s actual views would be more analogous to type A physicalism, since he thought that everything could (in principle) be discovered through reason alone.

5

Something like this has happened to some extent for me for and ’s anthropic argument. Each step of the argument itself seemed plausible enough on the merits, but as a whole it just seemed sort of disconnected from theism. But over time the fact of my existence has seemed to be more intuitive evidence for theism.

item.title: In Defense of Seitanism
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
It seems Miracle Discourse™ has finally fizzled out. I thought I’d take this great opportunity to introduce you to a religion of my own, for which I’m a devout evangelist. The miracle it is based upon is perfectly naturally explicable, and yet never fails to amaze me.

I’m of course talking about Seitanism—the religion dedicated to eating lots of delicious Seitan. The central miracle is the miracle of Seitan; this is the miracle of how a single food can be so amazing. In this post I will do my darndest to convert you.

Also, continuing the proud tradition of moonlighting as a recipe blog, I’ll include a basic, easy seitan recipe for your convenience. And to break the notorious habit of recipe blogs burying their recipes under 50 meters of text, I’ll give it to you right here, and then explain why you should care below it:

What Is Seitan?

Seitan is a protein source—similar to, say tofu—made from wheat flour where most of the starch has been washed away, leaving the gluten proteins. This gives it a high protein content, and a texture similar to real meat—often compared with chicken. Allegedly some vegans and vegetarians avoid it because it’s too realistic.1 Even if that’s not true, the fact that someone would say it in the first place tells you something.

It originates from Asia some 1,5 millennia ago with Buddhist monks, though it’s only within the last couple of centuries that it has made its way to the west. What a shame that is!

The traditional method involves making a dough of wheat and then washing out the starch over several hours. You can still do that (see e.g. this recipe)—in fact it has an even better texture, and is incredibly cheap to do!2 But it also takes a lot of time, so nowadays you can buy flour that has already been washed (called Vital Wheat Gluten), so that you just have to mix it, as in the above recipe. It can then be prepared a number of ways, such as steaming (as above), boiling, frying, baking, etc.

You can also find it in various grocery stores, but I find that the store bought stuff is not as good as what you can make yourself—and it’s also more expensive.

Why Should I Care?

Seitan is truly an incredible food, for a number of reasons.

It tastes incredible

Generally, I don’t like to compare vegetarian and vegan food to meat, as you’ll just get your hopes up and be disappointed if you’re looking for something that compares to the real thing.3

But seitan breaks this rule: It’s just so incredibly good! If anything it exceeds its animalistic comparison.

The texture is very good. With vital wheat gluten it’s not quite as fibrous as meat, but on the other hand it’s very succulent. Additionally it browns super well—arguably better than most meat—giving it a nice crispy outside and tender inside. And it’s pretty hard to mess up.

Now, it’s rather neutral in flavor on its own. But it has the benefit of being homemade, meaning you can add whatever flavor to it you want—not unlike marinating, except the flavor isn’t just on the outside.

I have often had people be surprised to find out that what I served them wasn’t meat—and I have had several people say that they in fact prefer the taste of seitan to that of meat.

If you compare seitan to the most excellent grass-fed wagyu Michelin bla bla bla steak, it probably won’t compare. But for a standard everyday meal, seitan is usually at least as good, in my humble estimation.

It’s super cheap

The main ingredient other than water is vital wheat gluten. Maybe you can find it in some local store, but otherwise you can easily get it for cheap online. Here’s the first listing that came up on Amazon, which is a 2lb bag for $22.

If you go with the producer’s serving size of 30g (23g protein), you’ll get 30 servings, which gives you $0.73 per serving. If you go with my more generous 50g (38.5g protein) I used in the recipe, then we get $1.22 per serving.

If going with the most basic recipe, all else you need is salt and water, which is negligible in price. The spices should pretty much also disappear into the insignificant digits—the only thing that is notable is perhaps soy sauce, which might add a few cents. And, you know, if you use saffron or something, I guess.

For comparison, I asked ChatGPT to collect price data, and information about servings. The serving sized aren’t all 4, because 1) some of these include bones, which have to be subtracted, and 2) the serving is calculated based on how much it yields when cooked, so loss from cooking is accounted for.4

When we look at this, it’s clear that with the producer’s serving size, seitan comfortably beats out all of the competition. If we use my more generous serving size of 50g, which got us $1.22 per serving, we’re still only barely edged out by the absolutely cheapest option.

Now, these servings are based on cooked weight, but you might wonder whether comparing the raw ingredients to the cooked meat is fair. As I mention in my recipe, doing 50g VWG per serving gives around 4oz of dough per serving—but that’s before steaming, which adds additional weight due to the seitan soaking up more moisture.

A more direct comparison might be comparing with the amount of protein per serving. So I asked ChatGPT for a table that gives us price per 23g protein (which is what we got for $0.73 of seitan):

When we make this comparison, we can see that our prices fall a little. But it also becomes clear that at these prices, seitan provides protein more cheaply than any of the meats in this comparison.

It of course requires some extra work to make in the first place, which you might value. But you can make it in big batches and freeze it down, which severely cuts down the work. And besides, you save some hassle in the other end, as it’s far less messy to work with and you don’t have to worry about hygiene with separate cutting boards and whatnot.

It’s easy to prepare in bulk

Speaking of, one of the benefits of seitan is how convenient it is. Once you’ve tried it a time or two, it takes maybe 1 hour tops to make a batch—most of that being passive time where you let the seitan steam. You can easily make batches of 10 or 20 portions at a time. Once you’ve done that, you get neatly portioned off lumps of seitan that you can freeze down and take out whenever you need.

And it freezes incredibly well! Once it has been steamed, it’s very resilient, so the texture won’t get worse. On top of that, it’s much easier than meat to reheat. You can just pop it in the microwave and give it 30 seconds, turn it and give it 30 seconds more, and it should be ready. Compared to meat you have to worry quite a bit less about uneven heating, unsafe temperatures, etc.

This means that it’s perfect for quickly throwing together a meal if you’re uninspired or in a hurry, since you can just whip out a portion from your stash and have it ready in a few minutes.

It’s healthier than meat

Saying that one thing is categorically “healthier” than another is of course fraught! How “healthy” something is depends on who you are, what else you consume and do, how much of it you consume, etc., etc. I wasn’t able to find any studies specifically testing the health outcomes of seitan in comparison with meat (please tell me if you can find any).

But with both of those qualifications out of the way, the comparison looks pretty one-sided if you just look at the merits.

Seitan of course has at least as high protein content as meat. At the same time it is very low in fat (depending of course on how much oil you add), has no cholesterol, and has essentially no saturated fat—meaning it also has fewer calories per serving. It also has quite a bit of iron (though it’s non-heme iron, so it might be a good idea to combine with vitamin C for better absorption).

Pretty much the only points where meat clearly wins is that it has vitamin B12, and that people with celiac disease or wheat allergy can eat it.

It’s not meat

Now, it’s no secret that part of the reason why I’m an evangelist for Big Seitan is that I care about animal welfare. Now, I’m not really too weird in this respect. Most people care about animal welfare—most people find it abhorrent to kill dogs for no reason. Not only that, the vast majority of people think that the way we treat the animals we eat is unacceptable.

The part that most people don’t agree with—or at least don’t act on—is that this means that we should change the way we eat to reflect that. I won’t try to argue with you about that here. All I will say is that the fact that the chicken you eat was treated in a way you find completely unacceptable—comparable to torture—should at least be some weight on the scales.

The main reason people give for not being vegetarian or vegan is that it’s inconvenient or doesn’t taste as good. If I’m to be trusted on the above points, then that is decidedly not true when it comes to seitan.

I’m not suggesting that you eat seitan all the time, or that you never eat meat again. But if it’s good to go vegan, then replacing your meat with seitan for 1 out of 5 meals is 20% as good as going vegan. I sincerely implore you to let this consideration have some weight in your decision about what to have for dinner—especially when seitan is not even a “downgrade.”

If this sounds at all appealing to you, I highly encourage you to try you hand with seitan at least once!

You don’t have to be a vegan, vegetarian, or soyboy to eat seitan. You could simply be someone who wants their food to be cheap, easy, and healthy while being tasty—and isn’t that all of us? I would definitely still eat lots of seitan, were I not vegan.

Objections

Still, you might have some reservations left before fully embracing Seitanism. Let me try and address those here.

It tastes bland

I have seen a few people online make this complaint. The best explanation I can come up with for this is that they’re poor cooks. If you do not put any flavoring into a substance consisting of essentially plain flour, don’t be surprised when it doesn’t taste of much. But I have simply never had this problem whatsoever—if anything seitan, when seasoned properly, has a very rich taste.

So if you follow the advice I give in my recipe, and make sure to season, sear, and sauce up your seitan well, I can give my guarantee that this will not be a problem.

It has a gluteny taste

Seitan, being primarily gluten, does taste like… gluten. This might be a slightly unfamiliar to you at first. But I have a couple words of reassurance:

  1. It is not really an inherently “bad” taste. What I mean is that after tasting it a couple of times, you probably won’t mind, unlike with burnt bread, or, i don’t know, feces. The problem is simply that it is a new taste.

  2. I have not found this to be a problem if I season it well.

Not a complete protein

Seitan is not a “complete protein” in the sense that it does not contain high amounts of all essential amino acids. Specifically, like most grains, it contains low amounts of lysine.

This might be a problem for you if your protein intake consisted entirely of seitan and pasta. But if you’re in the target audience for this post, your seitan-based protein intake will be substantially lower than 100%.

And luckily for you, pretty much every single protein source other than grains has high amounts of lysine. So as long as you occasionally eat some legumes, or milk, or meat, or anything else whatsoever, this will not be a problem for you.

Imperfect absorption

One thing people will often say about plant proteins is that they have lower absorption rates of protein than animalistic proteins. Now, this is true as a general rule, since plant proteins are in general whole foods (which is, you know, not much of an indictment in itself).

But it’s not really true for more processed plant proteins such as tofu and seitan. In fact seitan (as well as tofu, soya milk and pea emulsion) seems to be as digestible as animalistic proteins.

I am “gluten intolerant”

Okay, fair enough… but have you tried being a little more tolerant, you bigot?

Conclusion

Perhaps seitan is not a superfood in the traditional sense—there are healthier foods out there. But it is a food that is super! And in my estimation it’s as good or better than meat in almost any respect you might care about. If you’re eating meat, you might as well eat seitan sometimes too!

Gluten intolerant people go away! Everybody else subscribe:

A bistable mechanism is a device that has two different stable equilibria, separated by an unstable high-energy peak. A classic example is the light switch: It’s stable when in the off-position, and it’s stable in the on-position, but try and force it to stay in-between, and you’ll have a hard time.

I find my philosophical worldview is similar to a bistable mechanism. There are two very different systems of views, each of which I find quite plausible. But while they each hang together very well on their own, mixing them is not so easy a task.

item.title: AI Doomerism Is Not Bullshit
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
No more is the idea of AI killing us all confined to chronically online fedora-clad nerds. Since the hugging face attack, as well as the resignation of Jacob Coxon, talk of AI doom has infiltrated the mainstream discussion, and is now a serious topic in respectable news outlets. This may sound worrying to some.

In response to this, —author of Everything is Bullshit—published a new and improved version of his old post called AI Doomerism Is Bullshit, but in the name of cordiality called it AI Is Not the End of the World.

In the post, Pinsof lays out 11 underlying assumptions of AI doomerism:

  1. Intelligence is one thing.

  2. It’s inside of your head.

  3. It’s on a single continuum, from super-dumb to super-smart.

  4. It can help you achieve any goal.

  5. It has barely any limits or constraints.

  6. AIs have it.

  7. AIs have been getting more of it.

  8. AIs will soon get more of it than us.

  9. Such a superhuman AI will become better than us at providing every good or service in the economy.

  10. And it will become capable of destroying humanity.

  11. And it will indirectly want to destroy humanity, because destroying humanity would be a good way to achieve any of its goals.

He then goes through each one, attempting to poke holes in it, until it holds no water. In the end, his explanation for why AI doomerism is taken seriously by otherwise intelligent people is that they have succumbed to the oldest trick in the book, and reified “intelligence” into something almost supernatural—not unlike a ghost.

I quite enjoyed the post, and found it pretty entertaining. Although I won’t assume familiarity with it here. And as you can probably guess by the existence of the very post you are currently reading, there were also large parts that I found to be unconvincing.

Now, I don’t really consider myself an “AI doomer.” I certainly don’t consider myself part of the social group, and find the rationalist movement somewhat offputting in various respects. I don’t have any precise P(Doom), as I’m just too uncertain—and even if I weren’t, I don’t like putting precise percentages on my beliefs. However, if all you mean by “AI doomer” is someone who thinks there’s a non-negligible chance that AI will kill us or be otherwise catastrophic, and who thinks that it’s an important global issue to prevent this, then I suppose I’m guilty.

Anyways, this won’t be a thorough point-by-point response to Pinsof’s 7500 word post. Rather it’ll mostly be some general considerations, with a couple of more specific points.

My main complaint with the piece was that it was in large parts—how do I say this—a little too “academic.”

What Is Intelligence?

Specifically, I mean that a lot of it seemed to involve reading too strong commitments into the case for AI risk, and focusing on various conceptual issues that aren’t relevant to the core of the issue. Don’t get me wrong, I’m a philosophy-guy—I love all these sorts of conceptual questions, so I’m not one to talk—but it simply doesn’t seem too pertinent to the discussion at hand.

His first five points are perhaps the best illustration of this. They each involve—to varying extents—examining the concept of “intelligence,” how coherent it is, and whether it can do the work that the AI doomers need it to do.

I found parts of this somewhat interesting, but I’ll just be blunt: Most of it was entirely irrelevant to the practical question at hand. Large parts involved pointing out how the concept of intelligence is really an umbrella term for a whole bunch of more or less connected attributes of human cognition. We have attention, awareness, social understanding, emotions, etc., etc. Which of these exactly is the core of “intelligence” is not clear. Pinsof goes on to say:

We have a problem here, folks. The word “intelligence” is a semantic catastrophe. Whenever doomers use this word, I have no idea what they’re talking about. I often wonder if they’re talking about a real thing at all. And when they say things like, “AIs are approaching human-level intelligence,” I start to bang my head against the table. What could that possibly mean?

Now, God, in his infinite wisdom, created people with various levels of understanding. But “no idea?” I mean, the word “intelligence” certainly isn’t some paragon of clarity, as Pinsof aptly demonstrates. But, really? I mean, hardly any of our words are exactly clear once you zoom into the edges, but surely he has some idea of what people mean when they talk about intelligence. If not, I invite him to compare the problem-solving skills of a housefly—or a human baby, for that matter—to those of a perfectly normal adult, and I think the idea may start to emerge in all its vagueness.

A similar point he makes is that intelligence is plausibly a multi-dimensional thing, such that there’s no clear scale where we can rank every creature in the world from most to least intelligent (or the other direction, if you prefer).

This sort of objection has always struck me as, well, academic—to reuse a perfectly good word. Suppose you and I were were considering whether to piss off some muscular hunk in front of us. The following exchange might unfold:

You: Uh, I really think we shouldn’t mess with that guy. He looks plenty strong to snap each of us in half without breaking a sweat.

I: “Strong?” “Strong,” you say? I don’t really understand what you mean. There are all sorts of ways in which someone might be strong. There’s peak output. Then there’s average output over time, not to mention overall endurance. And if we’re a little looser, we may also include toughness or durability.

You: That seems sort of besides the point. Surely you know pretty much what I mean. Besides, that guy ranks higher than us on every single one of those dimensions!

Pinsof rejects this comparison. After all, we can measure the relevant strength in terms of a battle of fists. So perhaps we can measure intelligence in terms of a battle of wits?

But what if the very notion of a “battle of wits” is ridiculous—a source of comedy? Inconceivable! What if a bacterium could kill a chimp?

What if indeed… I mean, it may be too literal-brained of me to “uhm acshually” this, but we’re talking about intelligence here, so the fact that bacteria can kill mammals in a way that has nothing to do with intelligence hardly seems relevant. Second, I once again invite Pinsof to compare the cognitive powers of a housfly to those of a normal human adult, if he wants an example of a pretty one-sided matchup when it comes to a battle of wits. That there isn’t a perfectly clear fact of the matter in every case about who is more intelligent than who doesn’t mean that there aren’t some clear-cut cases.

This is all just entirely impertinent! Pinsof is supposed to be laying out the unstated assumptions of the case for AI doom. But I sincerely doubt that the case relies on there being some single unified concept of intelligence that we can all agree on. It’s not like the lack of a clear definition stops the AIs from doing their thing. What matters is that AIs have certain capabilities—such as problem-solving skills—that they clearly are getting better and better at!

The most egregious part comes when Pinsof claims that it’s a core commitment of AI doomerism that… Intelligence is inside the head?:

Okay, if we’re assuming intelligence is one thing (and we definitely shouldn’t), then it’s got to be located somewhere. Of all the places it might be located, your head is an obvious choice. Where else would it be, in the sky?

Uhh… What? What part of the case for AI doom relies on intelligence being “located” anywhere? This sounds extremely strange, and as far as I can tell, he never elaborates on what essential role this plays in the argument. Why must we assume that it’s “located” anywhere—it just sounds like a nonsensical thing to say to begin with.

You might similarly ask: Is my ability to jump located entirely within my legs? Uh, I don’t know, probably not? I mean, I also rely on my brain to be able to jump—and I rely on the ground, and on the force of gravity being what it is, etc. But my legs certainly have something to do with it, and it doesn’t mean that I can’t make meaningful and true statements about someone being able to jump higher than me.

Perhaps I’m being slightly uncharitable here, and the point of all these objections is more something along the lines of:

By using the vague folk-concept of “intelligence,” doomers are smuggling in their conclusions through the back-door. They appeal to the general notion of “intelligence.” AI has clearly progressed in some respects. But by pointing to the vague concept of intelligence, doomers can smuggle in the idea that AI will progress on all the relevant dimensions. It would be like if I pointed to the fact that Usain Bolt was the best sprinter, and inferred that he must be the best long-distance runner, since it’s all “running.”

First, if that were the objection, it would have been helpful if it had been stated. But second, even if we grant (as we should) that what matters are the more fine-grained capabilities, rather than intelligence in general, I don’t think the case takes much of a hit. AI has progressed rapidly in mathematics, programming, synthetic biology, etc. AIs are able to think and make decisions much faster than humans. And I hardly need to remind my readers of the infamous Huggingface incident, where AI agents displayed many of the relevant capabilities to some degree.

Notice that Pinsof’s objections are perfectly general, and insensitive to the facts. Even if we had the intellectual equivalent of the muscular hunk that far outclasses us on every conceivable dimension of what we might call “intelligence”—even if the nukes from Skynet had already been launched—someone could still point out that the word “intelligence” is vague and ill-defined. But that hardly moves the discussion forward. What is relevant are the capabilities that will allow an AI to overpower or outsmart us, and as far as I can tell Pinsof offers little in the way of argument that we aren’t on the trajectory to that.

The above was the core of my problem with Pinsof’s post. Now I’ll address a range of smaller points.

Evolution and Intelligence

Pinsof goes on to object to the idea that intelligence can help you achieve any goal. Now “any” may be a little strong, but it certainly seems that intelligence helps you with a lot of things—especially when combined with certain other powers, such as a body, or control over robots, or whatever.

The objection Pinsof raises to this is that if this were so, it’s very surprising that there are so few highly intelligent animal species. As he says:

If doomers are right about the awesome power and breathtaking simplicity of “intelligence,” then we should see a world teeming with superintelligent animals—giant brain-blobs slithering across the landscape. […] Where are all the superintelligent animals?

Doomers don’t have a good answer to this question. I often pose it to them, and they either wave their hands or shrug their shoulders.

As I said, I don’t really consider myself a “doomer” per se, but let me try to answer on their behalf. There seem to be all sorts of plausible disanalogies between AI and evolution that can explain why creatures aren’t all so smart, even though intelligence is very powerful. Here is one:

Intelligence is very powerful. But there’s a certain opportunity cost to develop it, since large brains are quite costly. This means that the stars have to align just right for a very intelligent creature to be able to develop. But once you do clear that hurdle, it’s evidently an extremely powerful ability (cf. Homo Sapiens).

This story seems plausible enough, and can explain why humans are so far ahead of the competition evolutionarily speaking, and yet why no other creatures have bothered to evolve high intelligence. And of course it doesn’t apply to AI’s whatsoever! AIs are being specifically developed to be intelligent, and so they don’t have to clear that hurdle. They’ve been born with a silver spoon up their ass, evolutionarily speaking.

While the fact that not all animals are braniacs presents a supposed anomaly to the case for doom, the fact that humans have absolutely dominated earth due to their intelligence provides an anomaly for Pinsof’s position that intelligence apparently isn’t all that useful after all—and a harder one at that, in my estimation.

AI Agents and Hugging Face

One of the parts of the post I found least persuasive was when Pinsof pointed out that AIs aren’t particularly driven in the way humans are:

ChatGPT doesn’t write poetry in its spare time out of an impulse to express itself. It cannot plan you a surprise party unless you ask it to, which would defeat the purpose. It doesn’t get scared when you approach it in the dark or when your mouse hovers over “cancel OpenAI account.” It just sits there passively, doing nothing. If you give it a prompt, it responds. And then it goes back to doing nothing.

That is noteworthy. After all, I have never heard of a human sitting around for days, hungry and thirsty, sitting in their own urine and feces, waiting for someone to give them a prompt. No, humans are go-getters, constantly doing things in service of their myriad agendas in every waking moment, often in defiance of others, and often in response to changing sights, sounds, threats, ruminations, and approaching antagonists.

That is of course true of AI chatbots. Because they’re… designed in a way where they can’t help but sit around until asked to do something? I don’t think anyone was ever really under the impression that a chatbot would destroy humanity. Obviously something that can only act for a short period when explicitly asked to won’t be much of a threat.

The thing that people are actually worried about is AI agents—AIs that act more or less on their own. Such as the agents that hacked a company without anyone noticing, with their only instruction being to complete a task that turned out to be impossible.

And when we’re talking about motivation or being driven, then the agents in the Huggingface attack certainly seemed to be so! The fact that they created a secret group chat, made an organizational structure, sacrificed themselves for the collective good, and hacked another company, all to make sure that they wouldn’t get caught cheating on a task they had already completed certainly seems like the sort of productivity most of us mere humans can only aspire to in our dreams.

On the topic of the Huggingface attack, Pinsof doesn’t really say much. He says:

Sure, the Hugging Face thing was pretty bad, and if you count the stuff surrounding that, then you get a flat line at zero followed by a recent, tiny uptick (which seems to have gone back down again with GPT Astra). Overall, it looks like 99.9999% of the time, with the exception of a few preventable fuckups, AIs boringly do what you ask them to do.

Yes, that’s true. But 1) the Huggingface attack was very recent. Had there been much more than one such incident in the past few months, that would seems seriously concerning. Oh wait, other AI labs have reported similar incidents.

And 2) it’s not that surprising that there haven’t been many incidents. Seriously bad incidents require a certain level of capabilities that we seem to have only recently reached. And if the rest of the doomer arguments hold, one very bad one is all we really need to be screwed—so the fact that “only” one or a few have happened so far is a sorry comfort. If Russia decided to nuke a European city tomorrow, it’d similarly be cold comfor that there had “only” been one nuclear attack since WWII—both because it’s bad enough in itself, and because of what it tells us about the future.

What Are We Even Arguing About?

To end off, I would like to fly up in the meta-helicopter. In these kinds of debates, it’s easy to get lost, and forget what we’re actually arguing about. The point under contention could be one of a few things, such as:

  • Is it likely that AI will kill us all?

  • Is it likely that AI will do something comparably bad to killing us all?

  • Should we be worried about AI?

  • Is the risk posed by AI large enough that we should spend serious time, effort, and resources on preventing AI risk?

Perhaps Pinsof’s arguments make a good case for a negative answer to the first two, and whether you should be worried is hard to give a clear answer to. But the only question that’s directly of any practical relevance is the last one about whether we should try to do something. In light of recent events, as well as the general case for AI risk, I think you need to have some very strong arguments, and be very sure that they work to be able to answer in the negative. And I must be honest that conceptual analysis of “intelligence” doesn’t really cut it for me there.

As I said at the beginning, this wasn’t anything like a comprehensive treatment of Pinsof’s post. I only covered the parts that stood out to me the most. I really, really hope that he is right, but in the absence of stronger arguments, it seems that this hope should be accompanied by a valiant effort to prevent anything bad from happening.

If you don’t subscribe and share, I might just go rogue and kill everyone!

item.title: The problem(s) with “The problem(s) with utilitarianism”
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Today, Econ-rabbit, published a post with the title “The problem(s) with utilitarianism.” It was in part a commentary in response to the recent Insect-Gate, and the public perception of Effective Altruism. The lesson Noah took from all this was apparently that utilitarianism is false.

I usually like Noah’s stuff, but this is the area where I’m the closest to having something resembling expertise, and I found myself disagreeing with a lot of what he had to say. So here are some semi-organized thoughts in response to Noah’s piece:1

  1. First and foremost, I think that people should stop suggesting that EA i synonymous with or implies utilitarianism, as that is simply not the case.

  2. Also, the argument for insect welfare mattering very much likewise doesn’t assume utilitarianism.

  3. A recurring theme in the objections he gives is that they’re ones in very difficult areas where no view is plausible. For instance, he points out that utilitarianism runs afoul of the idea that equality matters. It’s true that equality having intrinsic value is intuitively appealing. But doing so leads to the leveling down objection, where you say that it’s good to make some people worse off for literally no compensating benefit to anyone else. (Prioritarianism avoids this problem, but has other difficulties.)

    Similarly, he brings up the repugnant conclusion, and points out that the total utilitarian verdict that world Z is better is not obviously correct (or in fact decidedly unintutive). But rejecting the repugnant conclusion requires either giving up benign addition (making everyone better off and adding more well-off people isn’t bad), not-anti-egalitarianism (equality isn’t actively bad), or transitivity of better than.

    I don’t think this is just a case of “oh, well there are also objections to the other views.” The problem is that we know for certain that any possible view will have to give up on some highly plausible principle. So it’s misleading to only present the problems for utilitarianism.

  4. He says that utilitarianism has a problem dealing with death:

    If someone is dead, does that mean they have zero utility, because nothing matters one way or another to the dead? Or does it mean they have negative infinity utility, because lots of living people will try to avoid death at any cost?

    I think it’s pretty obvious that the answer is 0,2 not minus infnity. The reason people (rationally) avoid death at all costs is that spending all your ressources, until your life is barely worth living, is better than being dead. So if you’re self interested, you should be willing to give up everything to survive, until giving up more will make your life actively harmful. That, and people are afraid of death.

  5. He mentions whether future people matter. I don’t know that this is a problem for utilitarianism—he just seems to present it as an open question. In any case, I think it’s clear that they do. If you don’t value future people, you’ll have very strange preferences over time. You’ll accept a large cost to future people for a small benefit to current ones. But when those future people are born (assuming you’re still around), you’ll regret having made this choice, and will pay a large cost to reverse it. And you’ll predictably do so!

    Now, the person-affecting view is intuitive in the abstract, but I think it’s pretty implausible in the end—Parfit’s “Depletion example” is a good case here.

  6. Next, he raises the problem of interpersonal utility comparisons. Now, I think we need to separate two problems here: The problem of whether there are facts about whether one person has more utility than another, and the problem of how we know these utilities.

    If there are no facts (known or not) about comparisons, then that’s trouble for utilitarianism. But I think we can consider some clear cases where there are definite facts of the matter. For instance if I were cloned, so that there were two perfect duplicates of me, and we pricked one with a needle, and skinned the other one alive, I think there is 100% a fact of the matter as to who is worse off!

    The problem rather seems to be epistemic. But there being an epistemic problem is not a problem for the truth of utilitarianism—it’s only a problem for the practicability of utilitarianism. The right solution, it seems to me, is that we should have uncertainty about the welfare comparisons of others, and then we use the expected value. Now, for other humans, I have no particular reason to think that they matter much more or much less, so the mean will be that they roughly matter equally. For animals/AI’s it’s more difficult, and we’ll have to make our best guesses.

  7. Noah then talks about how there’s a difference between utility and happiness. The way he talks about this leads me to suspect that “utilitarianism” is used slightly differently in the economic tradition he’s from, compared to how it’s used in philosophy.
    In philosophy, utilitarianism is the view that an action is right in proportion to how well it promotes welfare. Welfare here is taken to be whatever makes someone well-off. Welfare is generally thought to either consist in happiness/pleasant experience (hedonism), satisfaction of preferences/desires, or some random mixture of various things (objective list theory).
    When Noah talks of utility, he describes it in terms of revealed preferences: Utility is just whatever people happen to want. But no utilitarian in the philosophical sense believes this (as far as I know). Even the most hardcore desire satisfactionists (such as yours truly) will say that it can have negative utility for you to get what you want, if it means that you harm your own goals (as often happens).

  8. Finally, Noah talks about how utilitarianism is good as a practical heuristic, but not useful as an overall theory of morality. Now, I must say that this puzzled me! Whether or not you think it’s a plausible moral theory of everything, this must be the first time I’ve heard someone (utilitarian or not) say that it’s a good practical heuristic!
    I assume the reason he says this, is that he’s an economist. When doing economics, I’m sure that utilitarianism is a good assumption for modelling purposes or whatever—a useful mid-level heuritic.

    But it’s certainly not a very good idea to use utilitarianism as a personal code of conduct. People—including me and you—are very bad at estimating the effects of various actions. I mean for an example that fits the EA theme, just consider SBF, who (supposedly) thought that doing a crypto scam would be good. As a result, he has become the public face of EA and all that is wrong with it, and has plausibly been the single most harmful person to the movement.

However, I do—contrary to Noah—still think that you could do worse for a moral theory of everything than utilitarianism.

And you could do much worse for a blog-subscription than Wonder and Aporia:

1

This was originally just a note, but it grew long and substantial enough that I decided to make it a post.

2

Or perhaps negative-whatever-value-you’d-have-gotten-had-you-survived. But I don’t think these are necessarily rival answers, as utility assignments are plausibly only relative between options. And if we were to have a 0-point, being dead seems like the best candidate.

item.title: Reductionism Is Eliminativism
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
In many areas of philosophy, reductionism is appealed to as a more austere alternative to eliminativism, which avoids the inflationary metaphysics of non-reductive realisms. For instance, you can be a reductive physicalist about the mind. By doing this, you avoid the crazy-sounding claim of eliminative physicalism that mental states don’t exist—but you don’t have to say that the mental is anything over and above the physical.

Similarly, you can be a reductive moral naturalist, and claim that objective moral properties are real, but nothing over and above the natural properties. You can be a reductionist about chairs, and say that chairs are nothing over and above stuff arranged chair-wise, even though chairs do exist.

However, reductionism is not a real position. At least, it’s not a real position distinct from eliminativism. There is no substantive difference between being a reductionist about some domain and being an eliminativist. The only difference is a difference in temperament: The disagreement is about how strict we want to be in the ways we talk, rather than about anything about the world. It’s a good old verbal dispute.

This is not meant as a critique of reductionism. In fact, I’m a pretty hardcore reductionist about most things—it’s just that I’m also an eliminativist. It’s rather a critique of reductionism defended as a more moderate alternative to eliminativism. It’s not, only because it’s not an alternative to begin with.

Coming to this realization has brought a lot of clarity to all kinds of ontological issues for me. It’s easy to get caught up in the question of whether X is “real” or not. Often times, however, there’s no genuine disagreement, other than a disagreement about how to talk. In all other respects, eliminativists and reductionists are on the same side.

A Basic Case

Let’s start with a simple example. We have a reductionist (Rhett) and an eliminativist (Eli) discussing the question of whether squares exist:

Eli: I don’t think squares exist. All we really have is stuff arranged square-wise. Once you’ve mentioned all the things arranged square-wise, you have mentioned all the things that exist, and don’t have to also mention the squares.

Rhett: Sure, you’ll have mentioned all the things that exist. But that’s just because the squares are nothing over and above the things arranged square-wise.

Eli: So we agree?

Rhett: No! The difference is that I think that squares exist, and you don’t.

This last claim is worth unpacking, as it’s supposed to be the core difference: An eliminativist, well, eliminates the entity from their ontology, whereas a reductionist keeps it, but reduces it to something else.

What is the difference here? It isn’t that once the eliminativist has mentioned everything that they believe exists, there are still things “out there” left to mention. If the eliminativist has a picture of some stuff arranged square-wise, and paints everything they think exists red, the reductionist will not have anything left to paint once the picture is handed to them.

The difference is rather what sentences they take to be true. An eliminativist will say that “there is a square” is strictly speaking false, whereas a reductionist will say that it is true. But the things that makes this sentence true according to the reductionist—i.e. the stuff arranged square-wise—the eliminativist likewise accepts.

So we have a case where two parties agree on all of the facts if we ban the word “square” from our vocabulary—they just disagree on whether it’s true that there is a “square” there. We have a word for this: It is called a semantic dispute. We agree on everything except how to carve up the world; if we agreed on only using the same precisely defined vocabulary, we could not find anything to disagree about.

And of course, semantic disputes are the paradigmatic non-substantive disputes. If something is only a semantic dispute, then there is no question about the world that is under dispute. All that is under dispute is how to talk about those facts.1

When the reductionist says that something exists, but that it’s nothing “over and above” the reduction base, that’s because that’s just how words work: When you define a new word, you combine old stuff under a single predicate. If I define “carage” as the pair of a car and its garage, I can now truly say “carages exist.” By doing this, I have not conjured a new entity into existence—rather I have invented a new way of talking.

Suppose someone now disagrees, and says that “carages don’t exist,” and that they’re not disputing anything about the arrangement of cars and garages. In that case they’re either using a different definition of “carage” (if any), or they’re making a mistake in how they apply the word. Either way there’s no substantive dispute here: We agree about everything about the world.

In other words: The eliminativist theory is true just in case the reductionist theory is true. They have exactly the same truth conditions—they are not different theories.

This is not a subscribe-button

Stepping It Up

Okay, but squares are a very simple and well-behaved case. What happens when we consider a more complicated case. For instance whether there are species. Let’s look at a eerily familiar dialogue:

Eli: I don’t think species exist. All we really have are particular animals with specific genetic relations, reproductive compatibility, evolutionary histories, etc. Once you’ve mentioned all these things, you have mentioned all the things that exist, and don’t have to also mention the species.

Rhett: Sure, you’ll have mentioned all the things that exist. But that’s just because the species are nothing over and above the facts about the particular animals.

Eli: So we agree?

Rhett: No! The difference is that I think that species exist, and you don’t.

Again, we can do exactly the same analysis. If they agree about all the arrangements of stuff, then all that is left is a non-substantive semantic dispute.

“But there is an important difference,” you might object. “‘Square’ is a well-defined property, so there’s no point in denying squares if you have things arranged square-wise. But species is a folk-concept with no clear translation into fundamental, microphysical facts. So adding species to your ontology doesn’t just redescribe old facts, but adds a new, explanatorily powerful property to our ontology.”

I might agree that this is another kind of difference than in the simple case of the square, but I don’t see how it helps the claim that there is a substantive dispute. There are really two parts to this: 1) That the folk species concept has no clear translation into fundamental facts, and 2) that having species adds explanatory power.

I think all parties might agree that there is no clear translation from species-talk into electron-talk. What, then, is the difference between the eliminativist and the reductionist? Well, it is whether or not to keep the species-talk. This is supposed to be a substantive difference between eliminativism and reductionism.

Let me now ask: What is the world like if we should keep species talk? What is the world like if we shouldn’t keep species-talk? Is there a difference? Nope! This is not a disagreement about any substantive facts. Rather it’s a difference in temperament: The eliminativist is less patient with vague talk than the reductionist. But how short-tempered the proponent of a view is, is not a substantive difference.

What about the second part? If having species in our ontology increases our explanatory power, is that not a good reason to admit it into our ontology? Or more to the point: Is that not a genuine difference between the eliminativist and the reductionist view?

No! Adding species does not add genuine explanatory power, by which I mean: Adding species does not help explain why the world is the way that it is. If the eliminativist and the reductionist agree on the fundamental facts, then they will necessarily agree about how the world is. Adding species to our ontology does nothing about how we expect the world to look.

The only sense in which it does add “explanatory power,” is by making it easier to formulate explanations for complicated explananda, like why this dog has 4 legs. But making it easier to say something is not a substantive difference: Adding “square” to our language also makes it easier to say certain stuff; but whether or not we use “square” in our theory is not enough to make a substantive difference, if they say the same thing about the fundamental things.

Now maybe there is stuff we couldn’t explain completely with fundamental facts. As points out, we can’t say what causes some glass of water at -10 C to freeze in terms of the microphysical state of the water. Had that state been different, then the water would still be frozen, since the closest possible world is presumably one where the temperature is something like -9.999999 C or whatever. What you need is some higher-order fact, like that the temperature is below freezing.

Similarly, maybe we couldn’t explain why a dog has 4 legs without reference to some higher-order property like species. Hence the eliminativist lacks explanatory power.

However, this just decomposes into things we’ve already discussed: The explanandum is itself a higher-order property.

If the higher-order property is itself definable in terms of the fundamental stuff (like “square” or “temperature”), then the eliminativist can just explain it by some long disjunction of fundamental properties.2 (Or they can coin a new word to capture the thing in question, but deny that it refers to a “real” property.)

And if the higher-order property is not itself definable in terms of fundamental stuff (like “species,” or “dog”), then we are back the the question of temperament: Do we want to allow these words into our vocabulary.

Either way, there is no substantive difference, or genuine advantage of either theory.

And regardless of what you say to these two questions, there is still a central challenge left: What is the difference between these two views? It doesn’t make much sense to talk about a reason for accepting one view and rejecting another, if they are the same view.

The only sense in which I can make sense of there being a difference is that they’re two different conceptual schemes. But, well, then they’re not different theories about the world as much as different ways of thinking. Again, the one is true just in case the other is true.

What Does This Mean?

If we accept everything I’ve argued here, this has some interesting implications for various disputes. The first thing that comes to mind is probably the mind-body problem. I take it that reductive physicalism is a pretty popular position here: The mental is real, but reduces to the physical.

Accepting what I’ve said, it turns out that this position is no different from the position that the mental does not exist to begin with! Is this completely implausible to begin with? I suppose if you’re an illusionist or the like, it’s not really, as you’d say that our experiences are just something like the brain representing its own internal states, and that there’s not even a conceptual gap here. From that perspective, it’s not particularly surprising that mental properties could in one sense be said to not exist to begin with.

But if you believe in stuff like phenomenal properties, but just think that they reduce to physical properties, it starts to look very, very puzzling, I must say. I did think that that the combination of phenomenal realism and reductive physicalism was in all likelihood false to begin with, so I guess I’m not that surprised at this result.

Another application is reductive naturalist moral realism. If you think that moral properties reduce to non-moral properties, then it just turns out that your view is substantively equivalent to that of a moral nihilist. Again, I think that’s an interesting result, to say the least.

Now, I’m not totally sure whether that means that you would not be a moral realist. All it really means is that you have no substantive disagreement with an error theorist. But you could still go in for something like ’s Pragmatist Quietism, and say that there are objective moral truths, but that the issue is non-substantive.

Now, does all this mean that reductionism is more radical than we thought, or that eliminativism is less so? I’d probably say a bit of both.

Reductionism is more radical, since the only sense in which the things it claims exist really do exist is that we can define the word “X” to make the sentence “X exists” true. If you’re a reductionist about X, then that’s in a sense all there is to the existence of X.

But eliminativism is also made a little less radical. Because even though you say that strictly speaking X doesn’t exist, you can still affirm the sentence “X exists,” given that you are willing to be loose with how you speak. Chairs still exist, even if all that exists is stuff arranged chair-wise.

Click on these pixels arranged button-wise:

1

In some sense, you can have semantic disputes that are substantive. For instance, you can have a dispute about whether the word “gold” picked out pyrite in the past. This is a question about semantics, but which is arguably substantive.

If we agree what it takes for a word to pick out something, then it is just a disagreement about, say, linguistic practices in the past, which is of course substantive. But in that case it’s substantive in virtue of being unlike the reductionism vs. eliminativism dispute, since there is actually a disagreement about the base facts (about “how the world looks,” if you will).

If we agree on the facts about linguistic practices, then it is simply a disagreement about what “picked out” means—which is plausibly not substantive. But even if it is substantive, it is again disanalogous to the reductionism vs. eliminativism dispute. It would be substantive because the question of which theory of reference is correct is substantive. But in reductionism vs. eliminativism, the dispute is not over theories of meaning/reference, but about the object itself—about whether squares exist. And that is a non-substantive verbal dispute in the typical sense, since it can remain even after we fix the substantive disputes about the arrangement of the world and theories of meaning/reference.

2

E.g., the water is frozen because it is -1 C or -2 C or -3 C, or…

item.title: Veganism Is STILL True!
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Earlier today (or yesterday, depending on where you live) of Lewis’ Lackey fame published a piece called Veganism is STILL False!, the conclusion of which I leave as an exercise for the reader to guess.

In it, he rehashes an argument against ethical veganism that he previously made, giving it a new defense, as well as responding to some old objections. As you can likely guess, I disagreed with his original article—and guess what, I think that his argument is STILL bad! And so I will argue now.

Arnfield’s Argument

Arnfield presents the following syllogism:

  1. It appears that we are designed to kill animals to eat their meat.

  2. If it appears that we are designed to Φ, it is not always immoral to Φ.

  3. (Conclusion, From 1 + 2) It is not always immoral to kill animals to eat their meat.

This is of course logically valid. Furthermore, premise 1 is plausibly true—at least I’ll grant that for our purposes. Of course, for the argument to be sound, premise 2 would need to be true. I must admit that I don’t find it particularly plausible on the face of it, and in his first post, Arnfield didn’t really give any positive reason to believe it.

That’s about to change now, as he tries to positively defend the premise this time around. We’ll see what he has to say about that in a moment. First, however, a word about the conclusion of the argument.

What Is Veganism?

A thing to note is that the version of veganism that Arnfield is arguing against is absolute veganism—that it is always, under all circumstances, wrong to kill and eat animals.

The problem—as he himself admits—is that this is not the only position which can reasonably be called “veganism.” But since it’s indeterminate where the boundaries of “veganism” lie, he is satisfied with having shown that one specification of the view is false.

Setting aside the issues of whether he has even done that, this dismissal is WAY too quick! The problem is that almost no one—certainly almost no one on this platform—who calls themselves a “vegan” holds to absolute veganism. If the “always” of absolute veganism is supposed to range over all possible cases1 then you can cook up a case like:

You’re driving in your car on a narrow road. In the backseat is your whole family, a scientist who just came up with the cure for cancer, as well as the detonator for a hydrogen bomb. A massive truck is tailgating you at worrying speeds.

All of a sudden, a fox jumps out in front of your car.
