You’d be able to stop just in time to not hit it, but doing so would have the truck ram into your rear end, killing you, your family, and the scientist, as well as detonating the hydrogen bomb, vaporizing a nearby village—though the fox will be unscathed.

You decide to run it over, although you weep with sorrow for the lost life. When you get home, you notice that the fox miraculously fell into the hood of your car after it died, where it has been fried by the engine to a perfect medium rare. All the passengers in your car are starving, so that they will die on the spot, unless they eat some of the delicious fox meat.

I doubt that any sane person would say that you act wrongly here by running over the fox and eating it. Yet the position Arnfield is arguing against is committed to saying that it would be wrong.

Even if the “always wrong” is only supposed to range over actual cases, I’m sure we could find some instance somewhere throughout history where everyone but the most brainrotted people dredged from the depths of r/Veganism would agree that it was permissible to kill and eat the animal in question.

I’m harping on this point, because I think that if the position you’re arguing against would be rejected by almost every single person who calls themselves a “vegan,” it’s an overstatement at best to say that your argument shows that veganism is false.

More importantly, the argument has no practical implications whatsoever, unless it also establishes that it’s fine to kill and eat animals in the ordinary circumstances where you find yourself eating meat. Presenting the argument as though it establishes a practically important conclusion, when it does no such thing, may actually be actively harmful, insofar as it makes you or your readers more comfortable with eating meat in ordinary circumstances.

So even if we grant everything Arnfield says, I would not admit that he has shown that veganism—in any plausible precisification of the position—is false.

Why Believe Premise 2?

Alright, let’s now consider Arnfield’s positive reasons for believing premise 2. He divides his case into two versions: One based on (Christian) theism, and one supposed to apply more generally.

Theism

The first argument for premise 2 is that if theism is true, we’d expect God to design us in morally appropriate ways. I’ll let the man speak for himself:

If you believe humans were designed by an all-good God, you will probably also consider it likely that their design is morally acceptable. This is not an ‘auxiliary hypothesis bolted onto’ theism. It is something we can expect to be true given theism.

Another way of putting this is that if moral agents were designed to go around torturing babies for fun, that would be pretty strong evidence that an all-good God had NOT designed those moral agents. Of course this alternative framing suggests that you can modus tollens my modus ponens in order to make an argument against the existence of God, but that would only work if you were already more confident about veganism than about God. I, personally, think there are stronger independent arguments for theism than there are independent arguments in favour of not-3. Therefore, I should stick to my modus ponens and conclude that [killing animals to eat their meat] is sometimes permissible.

Now, if we mean “veganism” in the sense that any reasonable person would actually affirm, the claim that the case for God is stronger than the case for veganism is approximately a 1 billion Scoville Heat Units take. If it’s the absolutist veganism of before then I would agree, but that’s not particularly surprising.

Bad Creatures!

In any case, whatever you should expect given theism a priori, any theist who looks at the world will find that it is in fact not the case that everything is fine and dandy all the time. Conditional on the existence of evil, the idea that an all-good God would create morally acceptable creatures starts looking to be in straight up contradiction with the facts.

There are all sorts of creatures that are seemingly designed to stain the world with as much pain and suffering as possible. An (in)famous example is the New World Screwworm—a fly that lays its eggs in open wounds, leading to its maggots burrowing into the unfortunate victim and painfully feasting on the flesh of their host. Whether or not absolute veganism is more plausible than theism, the claim that the design of such a fly is not morally acceptable certainly is.

I put something like this point to Arnfield in the comments of his previous post. In reply he said that these animals are plausibly not moral agents, whereas humans are. And it is much less morally permissible to create bad moral agents than to create bad non-moral agents. Or specifically: It’s more surprising on theism that there’d be moral agents designed to do bad things than non-moral agents designed to do the same.

I disagree! Here I’ll just steal my own old homework:

Suppose you are creating an AI system. You have a magic line of code that you can put in or whatever that you know will make it not just any ol’ computer system, but will make it a moral agent (and whatever that requires).

Now suppose that you are sure that it will do something bad. Do you then have very strong reason to not add in the magic line of code? That would seem very strange to me! Creating a creature that does bad doesn’t seem that much worse if it’s a moral agent than if it is not—I would think you have roughly equally strong reason for/against creating the system whether or not it’s a moral agent.

But God is in an analogous position.

At this point, we may just have to stamp our feet and insist on our intuitions. But I honestly can’t see how it is at all plausible that creating bad moral agents is so much worse than creating bad non-moral agents—to the point where the existence of the New World Screwworm is not that big of a deal; but conditional on the existence of the New World Screwworm, the idea that God would also allow moral agents like humans to have bad designs is so implausible that it completely swamps the arguments for veganism.

Genesis 9:3

Genesis 9:3 reads:

Everything that lives and moves about will be food for you. Just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you everything.

This Arnfield takes to be very good reason for Christians to reject veganism. I might actually agree with Arnfield here that it’s quite compelling reason for Bible-believing Christians to reject absolute veganism.

But of course, almost no one today eats meat that was sourced in the same way as meat was back in the bronze or iron age (or however much earlier this passage might pertain to). I’m relatively moderate in my vegan views, and think that raising some goats in your bronze-age village and killing and eating them might actually be permissible.2 Although I don’t know much about the conditions of animals back then, so take that with some salt.

Either way, most meat today comes from factory farms, or otherwise cruel farms, where animals live terrible lives. So it’s simply not comparable. If Genesis instead said:

Everything that lives and moves about will be food for you. Just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you everything. And if you end up raising these animals in horrific conditions, where they suffer in their own filth, never seeing the light of day, then that’s also fine btw.

Then this might be a relevant point. But at that point you’d probably want to do some exegetical gymnastics, in the same way that you do not want to affirm that the one who smashes babies against rocks is blessed.

The ‘Whatever’ View

Second, he suggests a defense that does not appeal to (Christian) theism:

The idea here is that if a creature has evolved to do something that we don’t like, we shouldn’t hold it against them and consider the action immoral - it’s just something they need to do to survive. We should just say ‘Whatever, live and let live’.

[…]

One way I put it in conversation with somebody was that it tugs on the thought that for something to be immoral it must be something you can change about yourself. Mosquitoes can’t change the fact that they are designed to drink our blood, so we can’t say they’re wrong to do it.

Immediately, there is a slip in the object of evaluation. The reason he gives for the view is something like ought implies can: If you can’t change something about yourself, it’s not wrong. But there are two facts that are true about non-vegans:

  1. They (being humans) appear to be designed to kill animals and eat their meat (this we granted).

  2. They kill animals and eat their meat.

It may be true that (1) is not something you can change about yourself. I would also agree that it is not wrong to appear to be designed to kill animals and eat their meat.3 But the thing that vegans take to be wrong is (2), and that certainly is something you can change. Let me provide the following proof:

  • Premise 1: There exist vegans.

Q.E.D.

The ought-implies-can-style reasoning simply does not go one inch towards proving that veganism is false. After all, the fact that you appear to be designed to do something does not make you incapable of not doing that thing.

Arnfield goes on:

In my original post, I considered the ‘Aliens’ objection to Premise 2 - there could be aliens that have evolved to do nasty things to humans and this could tell against 2. The ‘Whatever’ view deals nicely with this objection by just saying that the aliens aren’t acting immorally by trying to carry out their life cycle. The view would probably also license us killing the aliens to stop them.

Apart from repeating the above in response to this, I’d add: The phrasing “trying to carry out their life cycle” suggests that the aliens in question would not be able to survive, reproduce, or at least have decent lives without torturing and killing humans. But this is not at all analogous to veganism (cf. the above proof).

If we actually make it analogous to veganism, by having the aliens be able to live perfectly fine lives without torturing and killing any humans, then it obviously would be wrong for them to torture and kill humans—and any moral view that does not give us this judgement is clearly false.

Evolutionary Morality

Finally, Arnfield gives a closely related argument:

If you believe morality is a product of evolution, then you might also think that Premise 2 is true. The idea here is that that which is evolutionarily advantageous is also morally permissible. What is good for you in an evolutionary sense is what determines what is moral.

Again, this inference is mistaken. Saying that morality is a result of evolution does not imply that actions that increase your fitness are morally permissible. For instance, if morality is a result of evolution, it does not mean that raping someone is permissible, even though it increases your individual fitness.

To see this, consider two populations. In population A, people are generally self-interested. In population B, people are likewise generally self-interested, except that some individuals go out of their way to punish people who harm others, even when it imposes costs on themselves.

In this case, it might very well be (in fact it’s quite likely) that population B will generally do better than population A, meaning that norms will overall evolve towards ones that include punishment. This is despite the fact that acting according to a norm where you sometimes punish yourself is not evolutionarily advantageous for you.4

All this is to say that the fact that some action is evolutionarily advantageous does not imply that it is right according to the moral norms that are a result of evolution. Of course this doesn’t show that the norms that are a result of evolution will support veganism—but it shows that Arnfield’s inference is wrong, and so that the argument at least needs work.

Though let me add: If you think that morality is a result of evolution, you should perhaps still just do regular first-order moral philosophy. After all, our moral intuitions are the result of evolution, and what moral philosophy does is seek some kind of reflective equilibrium among these intuitions—that is, give the best coherent systematization of our evolved moral intuitions. So since first-order moral philosophy clearly supports principles like “don’t cause extreme harm for trivial benefit to yourself,” I think we can be pretty confident that the norms that are a result of evolution do support veganism. Though I’m not as confident in this point as the rest of this post.

Another view that might support 2 which you could group in here is virtue ethics - what you need to do to flourish is what is permissible.

This is also way too quick! People who subscribe to virtue ethics do usually not just equate “flourishing” with something like a thin sense of having positive experiences or whatever. Rather they bake the moral content of the theory into what it takes for a human to flourish.

To flourish is really to be a good exemplar of your kind (e.g. a sharp knife is a flourishing knife). Hence a sadist who goes around beating people up and enjoying this will not be flourishing, as that is not being a good exemplar of a human being. Similarly, we might think that a person who causes large amounts of harm for trivial pleasure to themselves does not flourish in the virtue-ethical sense of the term.5

All of this is to say: Adam Arnfield’s argument against veganism is STILL entirely unconvincing!

For each person that does not subscribe to Wonder and Aporia, a fox is run over and eaten—by whom we may never know…

1

Or let’s say, all possible cases where animals and humans have the same moral status as

2

Due to the fact that creating good lives is good, that consequentialism is true, and that such animals plausibly have good lives.

3

I don’t really know how it could be wrong to appear to be designed to do something in the first place.

4

You might wonder whether this trait doesn’t just get selected out. One proof of concept that it won’t: The disposition to punish needn’t be all-or-nothing. Suppose instead it’s a tendency that fires only some of the time you encounter a defector. Then what’s being selected for isn’t [punishing pays off every time you do it], but whether carrying the disposition pays off on average, once you factor in the indirect benefit of living in a population where harmful behavior gets deterred. The costly instances are simply the price the disposition pays some of the time, in exchange for a payoff that shows up elsewhere.

5

Arnfield also addresses some other objections in his post. But since those are not any I have raised, I will ignore them.

item.title: Being Vegan Makes a Difference
item.description: The causal inefficacy objection does not work.
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
One common objection to ethical veganism holds that buying meat—and hence being vegan—doesn’t make any causal difference for the number of animals raised and killed. “Yeah sure, we can all agree that what’s going on in factory farms is a horrific moral disaster, and it would obviously be wrong for me to treat animals that way with my own two hands. But when I buy steak down in the supermarket, I won’t change the number of animals who are killed—no one will notice one person changing their habits.”

This is a psychologically compelling objection. Thinking about the complex supply chain in the abstract, the idea that you could cause any difference seems almost laughable! It seems especially laughable when you’re standing in the meat aisle. “Surely no one would ever notice the difference if I buy one of these.”

However, no matter how intuitively compelling this objection is, I think it is as close to provably wrong as anything in philosophy ever is.

The Causal Inefficacy Objection

The objection in question is usually called “the Causal Inefficacy Objection.” The core idea is this: If you buy a packet of meat, or don’t, this will not cause any difference to how many animals are raised and killed. The supply chain is incredibly long and complicated, and simply not sensitive to a single purchase. Whatever you do will be way below the level of noise. But if you do not cause any difference, then it’s not wrong to buy meat!

You could maybe object to the connecting premise here by arguing that buying meat has other problems (such as reflecting negatively on your character), even if it doesn’t cause any additional meat production. But I generally tend to agree with this premise—and in any case I will just grant it here.

So the real question is whether our purchases cause any difference. As I said, it’s quite intuitive that they don’t. does a good job of making this vivid in his post Do My Meat Purchases Cause Additional Factory Farming?1 (here B is a world where you buy 1lb of beef a day, and NB is the closest possible world where you don’t):

In each of B and NB [the grocer] is in his office, seated at his desk, looking at the spreadsheets on his laptop. Everything in the two scenarios is exactly the same—with the exception that in NB the number in the relevant box on the spreadsheet reads “1426.5” whereas in B the number in that very same box is “1429”.

The odds that he’s going to react differently to these numbers is ridiculously small. He is exactly the same in each scenario, and he’s merely reading numbers that are ever so slightly different. 1429 is 0.18% more than 1426.5.

And this of course applies to every single step of the supply chain: At each step, some person or system has to first register your difference, and then decide to increase or decrease their supply in response. But at each step, your difference is far below the threshold of noise, so it will simply be ignored. You will not cause any difference.

The Canon Response

There is a standard response to the argument, that runs something like this: Suppose that some huge number of people stopped buying meat. In that case supply would drop roughly a corresponding amount.2 Now, due to the intermediate value theorem (or just common sense), that implies that there must at least be some number of people, where having one more go vegan would cause demand to go down.

It’s worth spelling this out a bit more. In the vignette Frances painted, it seemed pretty plausible that the grocer would not respond to the difference. I think this is because the grocer was not already unsure about whether to order more. Consider instead this case:

In each of B and NB [the grocer] is in his office, seated at his desk, looking at the spreadsheets on his laptop. Everything in the two scenarios is exactly the same—with the exception that in NB the number in the relevant box on the spreadsheet reads “1426.5” whereas in B the number in that very same box is “1429”. In NB, the grocer is extremely uncertain about whether to increase the amount of beef he orders. The demand is right up against the safety buffer that the store keeps, meaning the store almost can’t keep up if it doesn’t increase its order. However, they still barely can, so the grocer decides against ordering more.

In this case it’s not so crazy to think that seeing the number 1429 would have the grocer increase the order. And whether or not you share that feeling, it’s just a matter of logic that there must be some case where this is true, whether or not you find it intuitive.

After all, a sufficiently large step definitely makes a difference. If the number changes by 1000, then the grocer will certainly change his order! Suppose then for reductio that 0.5 can’t make a difference to the grocer’s decision. Well in that case, the grocer wouldn’t order more if he saw 1427 instead of 1426.5. Similarly, he wouldn’t order more if he saw 1427.5 instead of 1427, and so on.

Unless you want to deny that “more than” is transitive—in which case, have fun with that—it would follow that a difference of 1000 doesn’t make a difference. But that contradicts our assumption! So either it’s false that 0.5 never makes a difference, or you have to accept the contradiction that the grocer both does and doesn’t order more if the demand changes by 1000—again, have fun with that!

In other words, there have to be thresholds where some tiny change makes a causal difference. They don’t necessarily have to be evenly spaced, or anything like that, but they have to be there.

How big will the difference be? Well, we can’t say for sure. Sometimes the change might be small, sometimes it might be large. Hell, sometimes it might even go in reverse—human psychology is weird! But what we can say is this: If a change of 1000 will roughly translate into a difference in the order of 1000, then the average difference in order must be roughly equal to the average space between thresholds. So if there are 100 units between two thresholds, then you can expect that reaching that threshold will trigger a difference of 100 in order size.

This argument generalizes to each step of the supply chain, as well as the supply chain as a whole. After all, the argument assumed nothing about the mechanism by which supply changed, nor how complicated it is—so you can slot in the supply chain as a whole as the mechanism and rerun the argument. The sizes of the probabilities and differences might change, but the result is the same.

Now, you have no idea how close we are to the threshold. So you should give a roughly uniform probability to being anywhere in relation to the threshold, meaning you should think that you have a 1/n chance of causing this threshold to trigger, where n is the average size of steps between the thresholds. And you should expect that if you trigger it, you’ll cause around n more of the product to be produced. So in expectation, buying a chicken will cause a chicken to be raised and killed.3

Let me be clear: This “in expectation” is not some highfalutin mathematical abstraction. It’s not just that there’s some weird sense in which you technically make a difference on average; it’s that there’s a genuine chance you literally cause a difference, and the size of that difference is inversely proportional to how likely it is.

Objection!

I think this argument decisively refutes the causal inefficacy objection. However, there is a potential line of objection that can sound compelling. It goes like this:

The exposition of the argument trades on a bit of an ambiguity. When you say that there must be some number of people, such that the difference of one person will cause a difference, that’s true as a counterfactual evaluation. But it doesn’t follow from this that this ever happens!

Consider a simple analogy:

You have a scale that is sensitive at increments of 100 grams. So whenever the weight on it is above or equal to 100 grams, it displays “100 g”; when it’s above or equal to 200 grams, it displays “200 g,” and so on. Suppose now that you have a bunch of 1 gram pebbles that you’re piling onto the scale.

The above argument works here in a sense: It’s true that if you line up possible worlds in a row, such that you start with 1 pebble on the scale, then 2, then 3, etc., there will be adjacent possible worlds that have different numbers on the display, meaning a single pebble can cause a difference.

However, this doesn’t imply that there is ever an individual pebble that causes a difference. Suppose you start with 50 pebbles on the scale, and then pile them on 100 at a time. In that case no single pebble ever makes a causal difference, even though a single pebble could make a difference.

Tying this back to the veganism case, the analogy should be pretty clear: Even if one person can make a difference in one sense, it doesn’t follow that that ever happens. In fact, it doesn’t even necessarily make it likely.

Supply doesn’t respond instantly to demand, but to large groups, and over a long time meaning that the real world is more analogous to shoveling huge heaps onto the scale at a time, rather than putting on pebbles individually.

This makes it very unlikely that any individual pebble ever makes a difference. If we were placing pebbles individually (end of the supply chain noticing individual inputs, rather than counting them as noise), we’d be sure that individual pebbles sometimes made a difference, making the argument go through. But as it stands, your probability of making a difference is much lower than what the original objection supposed—after all more than the threshold amount of people can change their habits all the time, and no one ever makes an individual difference.

Reply

This is the best steelman I can give of the causal inefficacy argument.4 However, this objection is wrong, flaw being that the analogy is not apt—specifically the example of piling on 100 pebbles at a time. Once we fix the analogy, the Canon response still goes through.

The thing is, in the real world, we don’t know how close we are to the threshold, nor how many people have changed their consumption within the relevant period.5 Or in the jargon of the analogy: We don’t know how many pebbles are on the scale, nor how many pebbles are already about to be scooped on.

Fixing this, we can tell this story:

You’re a pebble who’s sitting in a handful of pebbles about to be put onto the 100g-interval scale. Being a pebble, you don’t have any eyes, meaning you can’t tell how many pebbles are in this handful, nor how many are already on the scale.

But you are a bit of a special pebble anyways: If you want to, you can jump out of the handful, so as to not be placed on the scale.

In this situation, how much lower would you cause the number on the display to be in expectation if you jumped out of the hand?

Well, since you don’t know anything about how many pebbles are on the scale, you should have a uniform credence distribution over the possible numbers. And since we don’t care about the absolute value, but only about where we are in relation to the threshold, we will take modulo 100. So we will turn 301 into 1, and turn 1546 into 46. So you have a 1% credence in each of the 100 possible options.

For simplicity, let us assume that there are 50 pebbles in the hand (we’ll relax this assumption in a moment). In that case, if you jump out you’ll make a difference just in case the number on the scale is exactly 50. So there is a 1% chance that you make a difference. And if you do, you make a difference of 100 (since that’s the step size of the scale). So jumping has an expected change of 1 gram.

What about if the number of pebbles in the hand is different? Suppose there are 49 pebbles in the hand including you. In that case you make a difference just in case there are already 51 on the scale.

You don’t need to be particularly bright to see where this is going: For any number of pebbles in the hand, your chance of making a difference is 1% (giving an expected value of 1). So when you don’t know how many there are, you can just apply the sure thing principle and infer that you will make an expected difference of 1 gram.

I hope that the analogy is pretty clear: When buying meat you don’t know how close you are to the threshold, nor how many people are buying meat that day compared to usual. So the analysis will turn out to be the same: No matter how many people are changing their habits today, the expected difference you cause will be roughly equal to the amount you buy.6

This of course assumes that you have no special information regarding where in the cycle you are. However, if that is your objection—and the reason you will continue buying meat—I will ask you to follow my instructions:

Stand up. Take off your hat. Put your hand on your heart and say in a loud, and solemn voice:

“I swear on God and my mother’s life that I actually do have special information regarding where in the cycle I am, when I buy meat on a normal day.”

If you can really do that, then sure, I guess you are fine. But if not, then I don’t think this objection will be particularly pertinent to what you should ever do.

Epilogue: Risk Aversion

So far I’ve been assuming that a 1/n probability of n units of value is equal to 1 unit of value. But this is not an uncontroversial assumption—especially when we make n very large. For instance, taking a 1 in a billion chance of saving a billion lives is plausibly not as good as saving a single life with 100% certainty. So you might for instance think that we should disproportionately discount small risks.

At this point, it becomes important exactly how large the distance between thresholds is. I asked Claude to give a guesstimate based on relevant empirical data on the various steps of the supply chain, and it said it might be something on the order of 1/1000 to 1/10,000 chance of causing a difference if you buy 1lb of meat. But, you know, take that with a large portion of salt—I just wanted to get a rough ballpark figure.

If these numbers are approximately correct, I don’t know whether that would be small enough to significantly discount the risk.

But let’s set that aside. Because I think that taking this objection seriously simply works as a reductio ad absurdum of applying the relevant sort of risk aversion to cases like buying meat.

The thing is, risk aversion may be quite plausible in circumstances where you’re taking a one-off risk at a very good outcome. But it stops being particularly plausible when the risk is constantly taken by a lot of agents, all the time.

Consider this analogy:

There is a 10,000-sided roulette wheel, that costs $1 to play, and pays out $10,100 if you win by betting on the correct number. If you were playing this alone, it might be plausible that it’s not worth betting on this (even setting aside decreasing marginal utility).

But suppose instead that you are 10,000 people deciding whether to bet on this. Additionally, you are not taking the money for yourself. Rather, the 10,000 people are all members of a club, and they’re trying to raise money for it. If anyone wins, they’ll put the money into the club’s bank account, and it will benefit everyone equally.

Considering this as an individual, the conclusion might be the same: There’s only a 1/10,000 chance of winning, so you should discount the $10,100, making it not worth it. But if everyone bet on different numbers, you’d be guaranteed to win, and so just earn $100 with certainty. So the correct strategy obviously isn’t being risk averse.

I take it that the latter version is much more analogous to buying meat. If you’re a moral person, what you care about is that animals not be hurt—that is, the goal you are valuing is shared between all moral people (just like the value of the club’s money is shared by all). Now, if 10,000 people decided to not buy meat, that would cause less meat to be produced (let’s suppose). If each person treated their decision as a one-off lottery, then everyone being “morally rational” would with certainty lead to the moral goals being undermined. So being risk averse in this kind of situation seems to be incorrect; you know someone will win (since changes in production happen all the time), and you are not special.7

The examples that make risk aversion seem plausible are cases where you have a one-off lottery with a very tiny probability of a good outcome—or cases along these lines. But this is decidedly not such a case, and in this case, risk aversion gives the wrong result. So a plausible version of risk-discounting should take into account something like:

Collective Difference-Making: One ought to take into account the choices of other people and consider whether the collective has a non-negligible probability of making a difference.

If that’s right, then discounting small risks does not save the causal inefficacy argument, since we are exactly in a situation analogous to the above lottery. The “lottery” is won all the time, since the amount of meat produced often changes, meaning we do collectively make differences like this.

But let’s suppose that this is not right. Even so, you still aren’t off the hook if you discount small risks. Because while each purchase may have a negligible chance of causing a difference, other options may not.

Specifically, consider the choice of going vegan:

Suppose that you form the firm intention to no longer eat/buy meat, and suppose that you have a reasonably high credence that this will more or less succeed—let’s say that you expect that this will cause you to eat 80% less meat (since you have a decent credence that you will stick to it. And even if you do “relapse” you have a decent expectation that you would still substantially reduce your meat consumption overall). Furthermore, let’s suppose that you expect to live another 55 years, and you—like the average American—eat roughly 225 lbs of meat a year. These numbers are just made up for illustration.

If that’s right, then deciding to go vegan will roughly lower your meat consumption by 10 000 lbs. Let’s also go with the pessimistic assumption that you only have a 1/10 000 chance of causing a difference—which will, per the argument from earlier—on average be a difference of 10 000 lbs.

If so, then your chance of causing any difference at all (i.e. a difference of at least 10 000 lbs of meat) is 63%! Surely you shouldn’t discount a 63% chance! The chances for various sizes of difference are laid out in this table:

If we did not discount risks, this would of course have an expected value of 10 000 lbs of meat. But we do discount risks for the sake of the argument. Let’s suppose that we completely discount all risks under 1% (although that threshold seems way too high!). If so, the expected difference caused still remains roughly 9800 lbs. That’s slightly lower than if we were perfectly risk-neutral—but it’s basically the same.

Now, there’s obviously a bit of a conundrum here: Going vegan would have massively positive expected value. However, if you don’t go vegan, none of your individual purchases have any negative expected value (with regards to animal welfare). However, that seems inconsistent! Which is it? Does not buying meat make a difference or not?

The problem is, of course, that risk-discounting views are sensitive to how you individuate options, since how large the chance of an outcome is depends on how generally you describe it. But that’s a problem for the proponent of the theory to figure out.

Unless they can give a positive account that solves each of these problems in a way that implies that eating meat has no negative expected value—and in a way that is plausible, rather than an ad hoc way of weaseling out of the conclusion—then I think a general precautionary principle should mean that you don’t justify eating meat with the causal inefficacy argument.

One thing I’m sure of is that subscribing to Wonder and Aporia causes immeasurable benefits to both me and you.

1

In that post, Frances is explicit about his being a claim about causation, that does not necessarily imply anything about morality. The response will rely on some assumptions about decision theory, which is normative. Nevertheless, the claim he argues for is the same claim that the normative argument against veganism relies on, hence why I think he is worth quoting anyways.

Also, he is arguing against the claim that buying meat will cause a difference. Depending on how you disambiguate that, it might be understood as buying meat almost always—or with near certainty—making a causal difference. This I too think is false. But I want to argue that in expectation, buying meat causes a difference roughly proportional to the amount bought.

2

Well, slightly less than a corresponding amount, due to falling prices.

3

We are assuming here that you should treat a 1/n chance of causing a difference of n as equivalent to causing a difference of 1. We’ll get back to that.

4

In fact, when I set out to write this, I actually thought that the above objection worked, and was planning on arguing for that. But thinking about it a little more, I figured out that it’s wrong.

5

The relevant period is the period between suppliers checking demand and updating their supply. In the real world this will probably be a rolling, weighted window. But we will just assume a periodic check. It will work out the same, since you don’t know when you are in relation to the checking period—if anything a rolling window will only make the causal inefficacy argument harder to run, since it spreads your effect out over time.

6

Again, a little less, due to falls in price in response to lower demand.

7

You might worry that this is just a standard collective action problem, and so it’s not really a unique problem for risk-discounting. But here I’d want to say two things:

  1. It’s not just a regular old collective action problem. The thing that makes collective action problems occur normally is that all the individuals have agent-relative aims. For instance, if you’re self-interested, you aim to maximize your welfare and not mine, and vice versa. This can create prisoner’s dilemma type scenarios. But if the goal is agent-neutral, this can’t happen! If both prisoners care about each others’ prison time as well, then they should both cooperate.
    But the badness of an animal suffering is a shared concern by all moral agents, and so plausibly agent-neutral (this was why the analogy had the shared club house). But with risk aversion, the problem is much worse, because everyone shares exactly the same goal, and yet acting perfectly rationally to achieve that still undermines it.

  2. Even if it is like a collective action problem, it’s plausible to say that in collective action problems, you should cooperate. If that’s right, this won’t help the case of causal inefficacy much.

item.title: Should You Act Wrongly?
item.description: This coming semester, I will become a big boy and be writing my bachelor’s thesis.
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
This coming semester, I will become a big boy and be writing my bachelor’s thesis. So far my plan is to write about moral/normative uncertainty: The question of how you ought to act, given the fact that you are unsure about what moral theories are correct. So on my vacation, as I was airing the dogs in the mild breeze of Lac d’Annecy, and roasting in the (not so mild) French (🤢) sun,1 I did not entertain myself with light fiction or a podcast. No, I was poring over decision tables and dominance arguments.

Upgrade to paid for the uncensored version

Why do I tell you all these interesting facts about myself? Well, when I reached chapter 8 of Ted Lockhart’s Moral Uncertainty and its Consequences (pictured above), I found an intriguing argument: Lockhart argued that it is sometimes the rational thing to do (i.e. what you ought to do under moral uncertainty) to act wrongly now, so that you may act rightly later. Reading the argument, I became sure that I had to write a post about it. Both because it was very interesting, and also because it was very wrong.

So in this post I’ll give a brief overview of Lockhart’s project, explain the argument, and then tell you why it’s wrong.

This post contains a lot of images, so it’s too big for email. Open it in the browser or app to read the whole thing.

A Bit of Background

So as I said, Lockhart is interested in the question of moral uncertainty—and as far as I know he’s the first analytic philosopher to give this topic any thorough treatment.2 In the book, he argues for the view that we should maximize expected rightness. That is, when we decide what to do, we consider how right each option would be according to the various theories you have positive credence in, and weigh that by their credences.

So suppose you’re at a modified trolley problem:

A trolley is hurtling towards 5 people tied to the track, who will all die if you do nothing. You can pull a lever that will divert the trolley onto a track with 2 people. Alternatively you can push a single large man onto the track, killing him, which will stop the trolley.

You are 40% sure of absolutist deontology, and 60% sure of utilitarianism.

Let’s say that the deontological theory says that both pulling the lever and doing nothing are permissible (right), while pushing is wrong. And this theory only has two possible evaluations: Right and wrong. We represent right with the number 1, and wrong with 0.

Utilitarianism is slightly more complicated, since it evaluates rightness and wrongness in degrees. To handle this, Lockhart introduces the Principle of Equity among Moral Theories (PEMT), which says that we normalize theories according to the options that they consider best and worse in any given choice situation. That is, we assign 0 to the worst option according to the theory, and 1 to the best option.3

So in this case, utilitarianism gives doing nothing a value of 0, and pushing a value of 1. Since doing nothing will kill 5, pushing will kill 1, and pulling the lever will kill 2, pulling gets a score of 3/4. This leaves us with the following decision table:

In this case, pulling the lever is the right thing to do. This also seems plausible enough!

As we will see, Lockhart extends this principle to courses of action, rather than individual actions. So how do we calculate the moral rightness of a course of action? Well, we of course simply do the same, and take the weighted average of the rightnesses given by the various theories to the various courses.

But what rightness does a theory ascribe to a course of action? Here Lockhart says that we take the average of the rightnesses of each of the actions making up that course. So the rightness of giving you a bouquet of flowers and then punching you in the face is the rightness of each of those, divided by two.

Alright, with this in place, we can continue to the actual argument.

Lockhart’s Argument

To argue for the conclusion that we ought sometimes act wrongly at one time, to act more rightly later, Lockhart gives us an abstract case. Basically, you are uncertain between two moral theories. Let’s say, as above, utilitarianism at a credence of 0.6, and absolutist deontology at a credence of 0.4. Also you have three times, t1, t2, and t3, that you’re going to act at. At t1, you can choose between x1 and x2, at t2 you can choose between y1 and y2 if you choose x1, and z1 and z2 if you choose x2, and so on. So you have a decision tree like this:

Now, let’s say that both consequentialism and deontology say that x1 is better than x2. However, if you choose x2 your later options are better according to the theories, overall.

Let’s make this more concrete. This scenario will be a little intricate:

Suppose you’re at a trolley footbridge. A trolley is hurtling towards a track with 5 people tied to it. In front of you stands an improbably heavy man. So heavy that if you push him onto the tracks, he’ll stop the trolley, although he himself will be killed.

A little further ahead, there is a woman with a heavy backpack full of valuables. The backpack itself is heavy enough that it will be able to stop the trolley. However, the straps are extremely tight, so she’ll not be able to get it off in time. However if you push her onto the tracks with the backpack, you know the straps will snap.

Yet further ahead is a guy standing with a rope. He won’t be willing to give it up, but if you steal it from him you can help the backpacker up. And if you don’t help the backpacker up, her body will somehow act as a perfect ramp for the trolley, so that she’ll be killed, and the trolley will jump over the backpack and still run over the five (you somehow know with certainty that this will happen).

If you do push the fat man from the bridge, there’s a policeman who will see this and arrest you. You can either lie to him or not, but it won’t really improve your situation much if you do. And if you don’t lie, you can either cooperate in the arrest, or not do so by hitting the policeman, which will harm him as well as make your sentence worse.

Now, as all this is happening, a kindergarten class of 10 kids is crossing the tracks. The children are not large enough to stop the trolley, so if they get run over the 5 people tied to the tracks also get run over. If you don’t push anyone, the kids will not notice what is going on, and 15 people will be run over. But if you either push the fat man or the backpacker, the kids will notice and avoid being run over.

For an overview of the scenario, I’ve filled in the decision tree like this:

Now, what should you do according to each moral theory? Well the deontology theory always suggests that you don’t do harm. So it will tell you to not push anyone, and let the 5 people and the kindergarten be run over. But it prefers that you push the fat man and then cooperate with the police twice over not pushing the fat man and then both pushing the backpacker and stealing the rope to help them out.

If we fill these verdicts into a table, it will look like this:

As for the utilitarian theory, it says that the best option is to push the backpacker and help them up with a rope, as that will only destroy the valuable stuff within the backpack. But pushing the backpacker and not then stealing the rope is horrible, as it’ll kill 6 instead of 5. Pushing the fat man is close to optimal, as it only kills one person (and we can say that you’ll only get a small fine if you cooperate). And the absolute worst thing you can do is do nothing, as that will lead to the 5 people and the kindergarten being run over.

Filling it in, it might look something like this:4

So what should you do? Well, if we use Lockhart’s theory, then multiplying all the paths out, it turns out that the best thing to do is to push the fat man and then cooperate with the police. The best path according to deontology is to do nothing, but that’s absolutely horrible on utilitarianism—and the best path according to utilitarianism contains two rights violations (both pushing and stealing). So the best compromise is to push the fat man.

However, notice that both theories say that pushing the fat man is not right! Individually, each would prefer not pushing. So the best course of action involves taking an action that is certainly wrong, in order to open up a path of action that will minimize disagreements between the theories later down the line. If that’s right, then it can be the case that you should act wrongly now so that you can act more wrongly later.

Not So Fast

As I said, I think Lockhart’s argument almost certainly goes wrong. To see why, we need to do a distinguish two types of theories, and see how Lockhart’s principles fail to treat them adequately.

Two Types of Theories

To see why Lockhart’s argument does not work, we need to distinguish two types of normative theories: Time-neutral and time-relative theories. This distinction generally tracks the difference between agent-neutral and agent-relative theories as used by Parfit in Reasons and Persons, but there’s no logical connection there.

  • Time-Neutral Theories: These theories are such that what your theory-given aim is, is not indexed to times. If you ought to bring about X now, you also ought to bring about X in the future, all else being equal. An obvious example here is utilitarianism: What you ought to do is not relative to when you do it. You ought to bring about welfare, and it’s not more important that you do it now than do it later.

  • Time-Relative Theories: As you’ll probably predict, these are theories where your theory-given aims are indexed to times. So what you ought to bring about cannot be determined without finding out when you are. An example here is deontology: You ought to not violate duties now—rather than minimize duty-violations over the course of your life. To see this, consider these two cases:

    • Modified organ harvest: This is like the regular organ harvest case, except that it was you who poisoned the 5 patients. So you can harvest the organs from one innocent person, killing them, but saving 5 others. According to standard deontology, you can’t do this, even though it would minimize how many rights you violate.

    • Future maniac: You’re mentally unstable, and know that in five minutes you’ll go on a killing spree, killing 5 random people with your gun. For thought-experiment reasons, the only way you can avoid this is to empty the magazine of your gun into another innocent person standing in front of you. Again, I think standard deontology would not allow this.

Each of these types of theories, taken on their own, could not license doing something they take to be wrong now, so that you do something more right in the future:

  • Time-Neutral Theories: If what you do now is wrong, that is because it will go against your time-neutral aims. But those time-neutral aims, being time-neutral, will already factor in your future possible actions. So the action you should take is just whatever action would bring about those aims, which will, of course, be part of the best course of action (barring a wrinkle we’ll discuss at the end).

  • Time-Relative Theories: Suppose here that you could take an action that, would be wrong now,5 but which would make you act more rightly in the overall course of action. Well, in that case, the theory simply tells you that you should perform the right action now. Sure, you’d be acting wrongly later. But the theory doesn’t care about that! So it can’t be the case that you should, according to the theory, act wrongly now.

Alright, so assuming these categories of theories are exhaustive (which I think they are), and what I have said so far is right (which I think it is), no moral theory could tell you to act wrongly now in order to take a more right course of action.

Still, the whole deal with Lockhart’s book is that he’s employing higher order principles about how to act under moral uncertainty, rather than applying first-order morality. So does this make a difference?

Is Rationality Different?

Here is a plausible restriction for principles of moral uncertainty:

If you are 100% sure about moral theory T, then your principle should tell you to act in accordance with T.

I mean, the principle is supposed to be about moral uncertainty. So if some moral theory is definitely right, your principle for moral uncertainty had better not interfere with the verdicts of the first-order theory.

In his treatment of time-neutral theories (consequentialism), Lockhart does fine with this.6 But his way of accommodating time-relative theories is a bit of a mess, and definitely doesn’t comply with this!

The problem is his way of evaluating courses of action as the average rightness of each action in the course of action, he goes completely against the spirit of time-relative views! If you’re an absolutist deontologist, you do not care about the average proportion of right to wrong actions over time. Rather you care about not acting wrongly. For instance:

A murderer is about to kill five innocent people. You have two choices, other than doing nothing:

  1. You can use an innocent person as a meat shield to save the two. Or,

  2. You can steal some metal sheets from one person, and some duct tape from another, and create a shield that will protect the five.

In this case an absolutist deontologist would say that both courses of action are wrong. That’s it. If it were to prefer one over the other, it would probably prefer (2). But on Lockhart’s principle it should prefer (1). The reason is that (2) involves two separate wrongdoings (stealing twice) in the time that (1) only involves a single wrongdoing (sacrificing one person). So the average wrongness of (1) is half that of (2).7

But that’s not what deontology would say! The wrongness of taking the course of action that is pushing the big guy over the bridge is not watered down by the fact that it involves taking a series of steps beforehand. Rather for absolutist deontology, the wrongness of a course of action is the wrongness of its worst link.

And this generalizes to time-relative theories more broadly! Deciding to take a course of action where you act wrongly is acting wrongly. What matters is not the weighted sum of rightness over time, but what you do now.

I mean, just to hammer this point home, consider this choice:

You either

  1. Murder one person and then kill yourself immediately. Or,

  2. Murder two people and then go on to live for another 100 years, where you do nothing but sit in a room and stare at a wall.

If we accept Lockhart's principle, it seems (1) would be a lot worse than (2). After all, the course of action is short, meaning the wrong action is a large part of it. However that’s patently absurd! Doing literally nothing for a 100 years does not make your actions any better, or make the total course of action any more choiceworthy!

Instead, I propose that insofar as we should evaluate courses of action, we should evaluate them by treating them as a single action: The wrongness of a course of action is the wrongness of causing yourself to perform all of the actions in that course of action. So the wrongness of pushing the guy in the trolley problem is not the wrongness of taking the steps towards the guy plus the wrongness of pushing, divided by 2—rather it’s the wrongness of going up to the guy and pushing him.

Why Lockhart Is Wrong

Okay, so with what we’ve got so far, can we be sure that Lockhart’s argument is wrong? That is, can we be sure that the most rational course of action is never one that involves an option that all of your theories deem less right over one that they all deem more right?

Yes! Remember, for both types of theories, you could not trade off rightness now for rightness later: 1) If the theory is time-neutral, then rightness later is already priced into the rightness now. And 2) if the theory is time-relative, rightness later is irrelevant. And to evaluate a course of action, you treat it as a single action, meaning you evaluate it by the least right action—meaning later rightness cannot outweigh a wrong action now.8

In other words: On neither type of theory can a course of action be less right than its first member—and one course of action must be at least as right (namely the one where you act perfectly from then on).

If this is right, then there is an immediate proof that Lockhart’s argument is wrong: If all theories prefer option A over option B, then by the above principle at least one course of action resulting from A must be more right than all courses resulting from B. After all, the most right course resulting from A must be as right as A, and no option in B can be as right as that course.

To diagnose his example, we need look no further than the table for deontology:

In this table there are several rows that violate our result from earlier—namely that no course of action is better than its first member. Specifically rows 5-7. These all start with a 0, but end up with positive scores. This is due to Lockhart’s faulty averaging principle. If we instead go with my principle and treat the course of action as a single action, then all rows that contain a “0” would have a total rightness of 0, since absolutist deontology absolutely prohibits you from breaking duties.

Lockhart Redux?

In the above, we saw that the problem with Lockhart’s argument was his treatment of time-relative theories. But what if I told you that there really is a way that what you should do now and which course of action is most right can conflict? Specifically if we change our assumptions about how to treat time-neutral theories. And what if I further told you that this actually shows a deeper and more principled way in which Lockhart’s argument goes wrong?

Well, I am going to tell you that. At least I am if you’re a paid subscriber. The argument above was my main aim with writing this. So I’ll leave this extra result as a treat for my paid subs.

This post has bonus content for paid subscribers. Upgrade to get full access.

Conclusion

So I don’t think Lockhart succeeds in showing that we should ever act immorally. Does this reflect my opinion of his book as a whole? Yes and no.

Yes, because I don’t think most of the principles he defends in his book are much more plausible than the argument we looked at here. But that’s hardly a surprise for the first attempt to develop a theory in one of the most difficult areas of philosophy. Philosophy should not primarily be judged by whether it’s right—it’s just as important that it’s insightful. And there I found this book great.

As an introduction to the issue of moral/normative uncertainty, I would recommend it. A lot of pages are spent on working through concrete examples, and much of that content can be skipped without missing much. But the theoretical considerations are still good, and the book gives a nice taste for many of the central problems in the field, as well as some of the surprising ways in which theorizing about moral uncertainty can give answers where first-order moral theorizing leaves us at a deadlock.

1

Yes, I did get severely sunburned, and molt my entire body. In case you were wondering.

2

I believe the Scholastics were interested in a question like this as well.

3

I think this principle is extremely implausible. It has also been criticized a lot, e.g. by our very own . But we will roll with it in this post.

4

In the book, Lockhart assumes that the expected value of an action on utilitarianism should assume that you act as rightly as possible in all consequent actions, hence why the numbers only decrease or stay the same as time increases. I do not think this is a plausible assumption. Rather the way you should factor future actions in is by calculating expected values using your credences that you will perform various actions, given what you do now. But we will stick with Lockhart’s assumption for now.

5

Here I’m assuming that the time-relative theory is indexed so that what matters (more) is what you do now, vs. other times. I guess you could have a theory that says that what matters is what you do in the past or future. I think what I say would still apply—though it’s hard to think about. In any case, I don’t know that anyone has ever proposed such a theory.

6

Well, not quite, but close enough (see footnote 4).

7

Also, his rule is extremely contingent on how you individuate actions—an issue he completely sets aside (p. 144).

8

There could also be hybrid theories, which I have not discussed yet, but which is relevant here. E.g. threshold deontology, where you both weigh rights violations, which is time-relative, and goodness of consequences, which is time-neutral. These won’t downgrade a course of action to the lowest common denominator. E.g. you can kill a person (intrinsically wrong) to save many people later.

This won’t change things though: With a theory like this, the “wrong” action is never actually wrong, as the value of the time-neutral part will already be priced into the initial decision, as with consequentialism. Killing a person is only pro tanto wrong, but it’s not actually wrong to begin with, exactly because of the later rightness.

item.title: "Preference Utilitarianism can't possibly be correct" Can't Possibly Be Correct
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, wrote a post criticizing preference utilitarianism. Seeing as I am myself partial to preference utilitarianism, I saw it as my moral duty to give a reply. Initially this was supposed to be a note, but as the reply grew and grew, I realized that I might as well turn it into its own post, and give it the space it deserves.

I’ll be quoting and summarizing Overmuser’s arguments here, to make the reading experience coherent. But I’d feel bad if I stole traffic from their post, so please go over and like their post and subscribe to them, seeing as you’ll have read their post too by proxy:

Overmuser
Preference Utilitarianism can't possibly be correct.
Preference Utilitarianism is often touted as the better alternative to the various forms of Hedonistic Utilitarianism. Instead of defining Utility in terms of well-being, with all of the difficulties that this entails, it strips it down to the more easily observable and formalizable concept of preferences. Utility is simply a satisfied preference, Negat…
Read more
2 months ago · 3 likes · 1 comment · Overmuser
Overmuser
Interested in analytic philosophy, economics, history, sociology, math, physics, and a bunch of other stuff. Basically anything that piques my curiosity. I spend way too much time reading.

Groundwork

Anyways, Overmuser starts off by laying out preference utilitarianism:

A preference is simply a desire. It need not be associated to any “feeling” of desire, it just needs to be desired. Thus, anything an agent wants, whether the agent is sentient or not, is a preference. These preferences can be ordered and compared, or weighed against one another. They can either be compared through time, or only in the present. For instance, an agent may prefer to have cake over an apple for dessert, and they can prefer to have it now rather than tomorrow, and they can also prefer to stay fit rather than get fat over the next year. All these preferences need to be appraised and ordered by the agent, both in the present and in the various time intervals that they need to take into consideration, in order to determine what they want to do. Then, the preferences of all the agents need to be weighed against one another, and the best course of action is the one that satisfies the greatest number of preferences. The most well-known form of Preference Utilitarianism also stipulates that all preferences should be weighed equally when making comparisons between agents. This seems to imply that the strenght of the preference should not count. I will examine the two possiblities anyway: whether it does or doesn’t count.

I find this exposition broadly reasonable, though there are a couple of points where I’d object:

  1. Overmuser says that preferences don’t have to be conscious/sentient. I agree that you don’t have to occurrently think about some preference for it to count. But I don’t agree that preferences have nothing to do with consciousness—or at least that this is any core commitment! I can say that for something to count as a preference, it must at least be something that a conscious agent is disposed to occurrently think about. So completely non-conscious systems can’t have preferences in the morally relevant sense. This will be important later.

  2. They also say that preferences should be weighed equally, and that this “seems to imply that the strenght of the preference should not count.” I absolutely think that strength of preference should count! However we choose to make intrapersonal and interpersonal comparisons, it should respect strengths of preferences!

Now, in place of preference satisfactionism as a theory of welfare, Overmuser will want to say that hedonism is the correct theory. This will be important as we go through the objections, as many of them are not just a problem for me, but perhaps also for thee.

With that settled, we can go on to the actual objections, of which there are a whopping 7.

1. Misinformed Preferences

Here Overmuser brings up the classic problem that we sometimes have preferences that are based on false beliefs, in which case it seems odd to say that it’s good to satisfy them—something that preference utilitarianism may seem to be committed to. They (rightly) dismiss this as a bad objection, though their reason is a little odd:

this objection is rather weak, and can easily be mitigated by adding a meta-preference that subsumes all others, namely that agents have to be well-informed. This would lead us to use some kind of regret-minimization algorithm to decide what to do, which is what humans seem to be doing in real life.

I don’t think this is a good solution (if I understand it correctly)! We can’t simply add in a meta-preference for being well-informed, if the agent doesn’t have that preference. We have to work with what we’ve got. And even if we do, having a preference for being well-informed doesn’t obviously entail that preferences that are based on incorrect information don’t count.

Anyways, I think the correct solution is quite simple: We say that only non-instrumental preferences count towards welfare.

Suppose I want a bite of a cake because I believe it will taste nice, and I desire nice taste sensations. However, unbeknownst to me, it is actually a cake made with dogshit rather than chocolate. In that case I won’t get any welfare from the cake, because the thing I really wanted was nice taste, and I only wanted the cake because I believed that it would taste nice.

With this view, preference utilitarianism is not committed to saying that preferences based on false information count.

2. Malevolent preferences

Next, Overmuser brings up the problem of malevolent preferences: People can have preferences that other people be harmed. In that case it could be good to torture one person for the sake of many other sadists. That seems wrong!

I think this is the toughest objection out of the bunch. Sadistic preferences are one of the things that make me most inclined to add further conditions to the preference theory of welfare, as it really doesn’t seem like sadistic preference satisfaction is good. So I’m not completely sure what to say here. If I don’t add this sort of restriction, then I’d probably have to bite the bullet, and then say some stuff about why the intuition may not be too damning.

However, this is the first place where it becomes important to remember that Overmuser thinks that hedonism is the correct theory, as this is just as big a problem for hedonism: People can likewise derive pleasure from seeing people be tortured, meaning it could be good to torture one person for the pleasure of the many. That seems equally bad, and so it’s not really any strike against preference satisfactionism in comparison to hedonism.

3. Contradictory preferences

Here the problem is supposed to be that we can have preferences for mutually exclusive things (even necessarily mutually exclusive things). Overmuser gives the example of not wanting to hurt animals, and wanting to eat meat. Given the moral nature of this example, a more apt test case may be something like: Wanting to go to a party, and also wanting to stay at home and watch a movie.

To be honest, I don’t see what the problem is supposed to be here at all. I simply think we should have the preferences count against each other in proportion to their strength. So if I have a 10 unit preference for going to a party, and a 7 unit preference for staying home and watching a movie, I get 3 units of welfare by going to the party.

At this point, Overmuser brings up Arrow’s impossibility theorem as a problem for aggregating conflicting preferences across persons. But one thing that’s important to keep in mind is that this requires preference comparisons to be merely ordinal in order to go through.

If you’re a preference utilitarian, you should not grant this! Rather you should say that we can make cardinal comparisons across persons. How to do this is another can of worms. I’ll open it very slightly, but only say a couple of things:

First, I think we can definitely make cardinal intrapersonal comparisons of preferences. The classic method is to see how large a probability of X you would trade for a certainty of Y. But even if that doesn’t work, the fact that this is something you have definite answers to in certain circumstances seems to me to imply that our preferences are at least interval scale comparable.

So what about interpersonal comparisons? Here I have a plan A and a plan B:

  • Plan A: There is some way of making direct comparisons, so that we can say that person A’s preference for X has such and such strength compared to B’s preference for Y. How this might be done is not obvious, but there may be a way.

  • Plan B: If that turns out not to work, we should normalize variance. That is, we calculate the variance of each person’s preferences across the set of options. We then scale people’s preferences such that everyone’s variance is the same (or perhaps we weigh the variance by how conscious the agents are, or whatever).1

4. Two methods of preference satisfaction

Overmuser now points to the fact that preferences can be satisfied in two ways:

by not having them, or by having them and achieving the preferred outcome.

This phrasing is a little confusing to me: Not having a preference is simply neutral. But judging from the objection that follows, I assume the idea is that you can increase net satisfaction of preferences either by giving an agent more of what they want, or by increasing the strength of the preference without giving them more of what they want.

We then get two cases, which we’ll tackle in turn:

  1. A person is dieting and tempted to eat a cake. Eating a cake will have negative consequences for them. But they could take a pill that would make them desire cake so much that it would outweigh the negative consequences. According to preference satisfactionism, this would be good for them.2

This is a case of wireheading, and I have come to the conclusion that the correct thing to say in these cases is: It is not good for the person to take the pill.3

Why not? Because their preferences are such that eating the cake overall counts more against their preferences than not doing so (as is stipulated into the case). Additionally, they don’t have any higher order preference for increasing their preference to eat cake (because they don’t value the satisfaction of their preferences de dicto). Or at least if they do, then it’s not strange to say that it would be good to take the pill.

Now, taking the pill may still increase overall preference satisfaction, if we aggregate preferences across all the time-slices making up the person. This is similar to how killing one person to save five may be better for the group of six people, once you aggregate their welfare together. But it still remains true that it is bad for the one person to be killed—and similarly it remains true that it is bad for me now to take the pill.

So taking the pill can be good from an outside perspective. It may be morally good for the agent to take the pill—they may be benefitting the aggregate of their time-slices. But it is still not good for them, as taking the pill does not promote their own preferences.

Note also that this example partly works for hedonism too: You could similarly take a pill that would make you enjoy the cake more. At some point this pill would be strong enough to make eating the cake better than not, all things considered. So again, it’s not much of a relative advantage for hedonism.

  1. You could likewise take a pill that would greatly increase the strength of your preferences for the present, compared to the future.

Much of what I say here will be the same as the above. But Overmuser then adds:

In this case, they would become like Parfit’s present-aim theorist, always doing that they most want to do in the present, and damned be the consequences.

First, I want to note that this is only a special case of present-aim theory. Being a present-aim theorist doesn’t imply disregard for the future—you can have preferences that your future life go well, for instance. Rather, it implies that if you don’t currently have a preference for something, then you are not self-interestedly irrational by not pursuing that aim.

That was basically what I defended above. Unsurprisingly, I’m convinced by Parfit’s arguments that the self-interest theory is wrong, and that present-aim theory or morality are the only plausible places to stop. Self-interest over time is one of many gerrymandered values, just like you could have what is good for the group of six people from before, or what is good for the group of me in the next hour, Napoleon, and some random duck.

Not acting for the benefit of my future self may be a moral failing, or something analogous to a moral failing, but I don’t feel any pressure to say that it’s inherently irrational.

5. Self-harming preferences

Here I’ll just let Overmuser speak for themselves:

Consider the following: an agent knowingly decides to self-harm (due to, say, self-hatred). The agent is not misinformed about the consequences of the self-harm: they know it will hurt. They are not inconsistent: they know that this is what they want most. They are not having any desire to not self-harm, thus unwilling to change their preferences to avoid hurting in the future. This person is, under PU, perfectly justified in hurting themself, and it would be wrong to intervene to prevent them from doing that.

This is fine. However, I don’t think that it’s very implausible. If someone genuinely doesn’t care that they are being hurt, and doesn’t have any conflicting preferences—if harming themselves is literally the only thing they want—then I can’t see why it should be bad for them.

There’s something a little ambiguous about “hurt” here. If we simply mean the feeling associated with, say, knocking your toe into a table leg, then it might be the case that someone doesn’t have any preferences regarding that feeling.

In that case I don’t see why we should think that “hurting” is bad. If I have that feeling, but am entirely indifferent, and no part of me is inclined to want it to stop, then it doesn’t seem bad to me at all.

If instead “hurt” is a slightly thicker concept, involving also a desire for the feeling to stop, then preference satisfactionism necessarily implies that it’s bad, all else being equal.

There might of course be someone who desires to be “hurt” in this sense too, all things considered. But again that doesn’t seem implausible at all. I don’t find anything weird about saying that it’s good for a sadomasochist to have hot wax dripped on them, if that’s really more in line with their desires, all things considered.

Now, in this case there is probably some other non-instrumental goal, such as feeling close to the dominatrix or whatever (not my area of expertise). But what about a person who simply desires to be hurt for its own sake. They have a brute preference to have experiences that they prefer not to have.

First, I’m not sure whether that’s even a possible preference to have. But if it is, it’s certainly extraordinarily weird—so weird that I can’t imagine what it would be like, meaning I don’t trust any intuitions I form about this case. And given that the other two cases turned out to not be intuitively wrong when spelled out in more detail, I trust that the same would probably hold for this if I could imagine it.

Overmuser then goes on to add:

Note that this holds even if “self-harm” is defined as “something that reduces their ability to satisfy their preferences in the future”, because it doesn’t change the fact that this is the preference they want to satisfy in the present.

At this point I think they make a mistake! It does not automatically hold even if “self-harm” is defined as “something that reduces their ability to satisfy their preferences in the future.”

At least, this is ambiguous. If the preferences I am prevented from satisfying in the future are some that I already have, or that I’m committed to by my own values, then preference satisfactionism does not say that self-harm is good!

For instance, if I have a preference to live a long and healthy life, but I also have a preference to stuff myself with chips and heroin every evening, this would count as self-harm under this definition. But in this case, preference utilitarianism does not imply that you should eat chips and take heroin! After all, this is another case of conflicting preferences. And if eating chips and taking heroin satisfies the collection of these preferences less overall (as is plausible), you should not do so!

This is a common mistake I see: People assume that preference satisfactionism is committed to the claim that it’s always good for you to do whatever you want to do right now. That’s not true! You can have preferences about the future, and have preferences that are not currently motivating. Doing what you want right now can conflict with the overall satisfaction of your preferences. Exactly like how if you want to have as much money as possible, it does not follow that you should immediately borrow as much money as you can, just because that is what will make the number on your bank account immediately go up the fastest.

We could instead disambiguate “something that reduces their ability to satisfy their preferences in the future” as meaning preferences they would have in the future, though ones that are not implied by their current values. If that’s right, however, this is another case of wireheading like the pill and the cake—and what I said above applies.

6. Absent preferences

According to preference satisfactionism, if you do not have any preferences, then your life is morally neutral—you can neither be harmed nor benefitted. This, Overmuser claims, means that if one loses all desires, one ceases to be a moral patient, according to preference utilitarianism.

I don’t want to be too pedantic, but while this is almost right, it isn’t strictly speaking right. It’s not that someone who has no desires is not a moral patient, it’s just that you can’t possibly harm or benefit them—but if you could, it would still matter. This may sound like a distinction without a difference. For practical purposes that’s right, but I think Overmuser’s framing makes this sound less plausible than it is.

The next claim is not nearly as defensible, however. Overmuser says:

Depressed people can literally lose the will to live, and stop eating, showering, going out, and sometimes even sleeping (although some can develop hypersomnia rather than insomnia). According to PU, a depressed person loses moral patienthood because their condition makes them unable to form preferences.

Now, I have never been depressed, so I can’t speak to the details of how it is. But I’m pretty sure that depressed people are not literally bereft of preferences whatsoever. There is a difference between motivation and preference: You can prefer something while lacking the motivation to go out and do it. I believe depression mostly harms motivation. Depressed people certainly don’t lack preferences entirely.

Maybe this is supposed to be some sort of hyperbole or whatever? But I can’t find anything to indicate that in the text.

In any case, Overmusers claim—taken at fact value—becomes ridiculously implausible once we imagine what someone devoid of preferences would actually be like:

If someone genuinely had no preferences whatsoever, then that would mean that you could kick them in the balls and they wouldn’t mind. If you started sawing off their arm, they would not object; they would not want the feeling to stop; and there would be no goals of theirs that they would no longer be able to achieve. If you put a gun to their head and threatened to blow out their brains, they would not have any preference either way. If they shat their pants they would not mind—nor would they mind if you cleaned it up. Does this sound like a normal depressed person?

Seriously imagining a person like this, I feel no inclination to say that it would be bad for them to have their arm sawed off, shit their pants, or be killed; or go on living, for that matter.

In fact, I think it is a counterexample to hedonism that it would (presumably) say that it would be bad for this person to be kicked in their balls, even though they would have nothing against it whatsoever, and would not have any desire for the accompanying feeling to stop.
