Next, Overmuser says:

However, depression is not the worst example. As I have written multiple times, some forms of pain can be so intense that they abolish moral agency. What I didn’t realize is that there are pains that do something even worse than that: they abolish agency, period. People can become delirious and unable to reason because of the pain. How do we take into account their preferences in this case? What if someone is in so much pain that, in the midst of their delirium, they ask for more? Did they form a preference? Or should an external observer decide for them?

Here we have to remember the two senses of “hurt” or “pain.” If the pain they’re in is the kind that they desire to stop, then it would be bad for them, and the verbal report would simply be wrong.

If instead it’s merely the feeling of pain, but their brain somehow clicks, so that they no longer desire that feeling to stop in any way (or even wholeheartedly desire it to continue), then I don’t find it implausible that it would no longer be intrinsically bad—though it may be bad for instrumental reasons.

Now, Overmuser also seems to find it problematic that it’s hard to know which it is. But that’s a perfectly general problem for any theory of welfare that makes reference to internal states—which includes all of them, I believe.

7. Who has the preference

The final objection is that non-sentient entities could have preferences. Overmuser brings in the concept of a Vulcan:

a hypothetical kind of beings first theorized by David Chalmers, that are not capable of sentience (no hedonic values, no what-it’s-likeness to feel anything whatsoever), but who are still conscious and capable of forming preferences (in a very narrow sense: ordered set of actions, ranked from most preferred to least preferred).

Hold on a second… They’re conscious, but they have no “what-it’s-likeness”? If you’re a phenomenal realist, that’s not gonna slide. In that case we’re just talking about philosophical zombies.

As I said at the start, preference utilitarianism is not automatically committed to saying that non-conscious systems have morally relevant preferences. In fact, I think that’s clearly wrong! You might object “oh, well per the definition of ‘preference’ they do.” Fine, then I’m a schmeference utilitarian, I guess.

I would only want to say that the morally relevant notion of preference is one that involves at least some kind of disposition to have a conscious thought about the preference.

But let’s go with the idea of a Vulcan as being conscious (and so not lacking “what-it’s-likeness”) but lacking hedonic states. So they have qualia, but no pain or pleasure or the like. Is it implausible that these have moral weight?

Ehh, I don’t know, not really? That seems totally fine to me! I mean, to the extent that humans have preferences with no associated hedonic states, it seems to me that it matters: If my friends are only pretending to be my friends, but I never find out, I think that would be bad for me. In that case, I don’t feel any pain from my preference not being satisfied, but it’s still bad for me.

Also, I’m inclined to say that what makes hedonic states valuable at all is the preference to have them stop or continue. If I’m in pain, but no part of me wants it to stop, then I can’t see how it’s supposed to be bad. If that’s right, then it’s hard to see why only the subset of preferences that are about my immediate conscious experience should matter.

Overmuser goes on to claim that this is especially implausible because it would mean that non-sentient entities like Vulcans could outweigh human interests:

The Preference Monster: a being (or group of beings) that is not sentient (it doesn’t even need to be conscious), but forms a very strong preference for obtaining certain things, like, say, paperclips. The Preference Utilitarian could, in theory, be morally obligated to allocate all the world’s resources to this category of agents, even though there is nothing akin to what we call “desire”, “pleasure” or “pain” happening in their mind.

Now, I think slipping that “desire” in there is a little suspect. I do think desires matter intrinsically. In fact I think that desires are the fundamental part, and that preferences matter insofar as preferences result from desires (hence why I usually say that I’m a desire satisfactionist—usually the distinction isn’t too important, but I guess it is here).

Setting that aside, I have two problems with this:

  1. I think it matters immensely whether the entity in question is conscious. And I don’t think stuff like groups are conscious (this will matter in a moment).

  2. Whatever implausibility comes from this comes from combining different things that are slightly unintuitive on their own: Non-sentient but conscious beings mattering, large numbers or high degrees of welfare swamping concern for others, and inequality being justifiable.
    This is no less plausible than the utility monster, or many small pains being worse than a torture. That is, most of the intuitive force comes from the utilitarianism part, not the preference part. So noting that this is an unintuitive result and putting the blame on preference satisfactionism is not a good argument.

At this point, Overmuser makes the most outrageous claim yet:

However, the greatest problem with Preference Utilitarianism is that we can literally stipulate moral patients into existence: for instance, suppose I stipulated that there be a non-sentient, non-conscious, abstract entity whose sole purpose were to hold the preference “people should subscribe to Overmuser”. According to PU, you would be morally obligated to.

What?!…

What?!…

The most charitable reading I can make here is that Overmuser is using “literally” to mean “figuratively” here. Even then, I don’t even know where to start here, or what this is supposed to mean. You decidedly can’t stipulate things into existence and have them matter.

Perhaps we can gain some clarity by reading on:

Now this is obviously absurd: you can’t just stipulate entities that hold preferences in the abstract.

I agree…

And yet, we have real life examples of such entities, with real-world effects: many humans were horrifically sacrificed to various mythological entities, for instance. Closer to us, corporations are legal persons that can have rights and obligations, and have humans act on their behalf. […] These entities are abstract concepts that only exist because we have decided to stipulate them into being at some point in the past, and that continue to have consequences, for better or worse, to this day.

Okay, so it sounds like Overmuser is just using “stipulate” to describe anything brought about by intentional human action. This is obviously absurd!

Suppose that I told you that I had “stipulated” a child into being. What I really meant was that I had intentionally had unprotected sex with a woman, who became pregnant and then gave birth to a child. Would you say that using the word “stipulate” was appropriate here?

Once we translate this, the objection—as far as I can tell—is that preference utilitarianism is wrong because it says that things that were brought about through intentional human action matter.

Uhh… Yes? That seems fine.

Now, again, I don’t think that non-conscious entities like groups matter intrinsically, and nothing in preference utilitarianism forces me to say this. So this objection doesn’t even get off the ground. Even if it did, however, saying that you can just “stipulate” things that matter into existence on preference utilitarianism is wildly inaccurate!

The solution is not just hedonism

Finally, Overmuser claims that the solution to all these problems is hedonism. As we’ve seen, that is not correct, as several of the objections apply roughly equally to hedonism. But they also give an argument:

Some Preference Utilitarians resort to an idealized version of the deliberative process in order to obtain a “filtered” list of preferences, one that is supposedly “better”. What is this filtered list? The one that… best promotes the agent’s well-being. In other words, hedonism.

That’s not accurate. Filtered list views much more resemble something like objective list theory, since they will still include stuff like relationships as intrinsically valuable (which hedonism doesn’t), but try to exclude stuff like grass-counting. Now, I don’t find these sorts of idealized preference views plausible or necessary, but they certainly aren’t hedonistic.

Now, at this point, Overmuser makes what I can only classify as a Freudian slip, handing the whole game back to the preference satisfaction view (half-kidding):

Any attempt to get rid of this is anti-human, anti-sentience, and doomed to fail for sentient agents. Why? Because we already know what sentient agents care about. All the talk about preferences is just a proxy for a more fundamental source of value: the hedonic valence. Without it, we are left with a morality that doesn’t apply to humans.

[…] We must take into consideration the things that we actually value, whether positively (pleasure) or negatively (pain).

Boy, do I have some good news for you: If you want to base your theory of welfare on what we actually value and care about, I have just the theory.

If this is genuinely the reason why Overmuser finds hedonism plausible, then I think they’re a preference satisfactionist who happens to think that our preferences are only for pain and pleasure.

Now, maybe that empirical premise is plausible (I don’t think it is), but it would only make hedonism and preference satisfactionism accidentally coextensive. If we happened to value some other stuff than our immediate conscious experience, this motivation should lead us to say that that stuff matters too. That is, we should simply be preference satisfactionists.

So I guess Overmuser and I do agree after all.

item.title: Giving What You Can
item.description: Leave the world better than you found it
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Aisha can’t breathe. Her palms are cold and pale. She presses her body against her mother, delirious and confused, seeking any comfort from the pain. She tries to cry but her voice is faint. She doesn’t understand what’s happening.

Like most severe malaria patients, Aisha is under five years old. A parasite is destroying her red blood cells faster than her body can replace them. Her nascent immune system was unprepared and was already weakened by malnourishment before she was infected by a mosquito bite.

Aisha was picking pink hibiscuses just two days ago, smiling proudly when she handed the bouquet to her mother. Malaria comes on fast. The disease is hard to detect and treat in small children because early symptoms mirror a dozen other common illnesses until it’s too late.

Aisha’s mother holds her and prays. Please, God. Please. Let it pass before the seizures. Give her any help, anything. She doesn’t deserve this.1

When you first hear Peter Singer’s drowning child thought experiment you’ll likely find it rather convincing. On the off-chance that you haven’t heard it, the basic idea is this:

You’re walking past a shallow pond with a $4000 bill (never heard of those?) in your pocket. Passing, you see something splashing about in the pond. Turns out it’s a small child who—due to his stumpy legs—is unable to reach the bottom, and is about to drown. You could save him by simply walking over, but since your pockets are very deep, you won’t be able to fish out your $4000 in time. So it’s the child or the dollars.

I suspect you’d think you should choose the child in this story. But—surprise, surprise—this is very much like the real world! There are charities that on average save a human life for $4000.2 So if you should sacrifice $4000 to save a life in front of you, why not when the only difference is that you’re separated by some kilometers and a button? In other words, it seems you’re obligated to donate substantial amounts of money to charities that are at least as good as the ones mentioned.

There might be a bunch of disanalogies you’re thinking of. Most likely they have already been discussed (see e.g. here, here, or here). But there is one objection in particular that is uncomfortable—and, I believe, a large reason why many people don’t act on the argument.

If I’m obligated to spend $4000 to save a life, then what about after I’ve spent those $4000? There’ll still be money in my bank account and people in need of saving. If I had to save the person the first time, then what exactly is the reason why I shouldn’t save another person, and another, and… Buying the drowning child argument, it’s hard to see how we escape the conclusion that we have to work 9-9 jobs to maximize our income, donating it all, until we’re just barely better off than the people we’re helping.

I would guess that almost everyone agrees that this is an implausible implication. However, note that denying the drowning child argument wholesale is no more plausible of a response:

You’re just about to wade out to save the child. However, as you reach the shore, you peek behind a bush that was obstructing your view. Behind it you find more pond, and hundreds—if not thousands—of children also drowning.

Were this to happen, it’d not be plausible to say that you had to spend all hours of your day pulling children out of ponds, until your life were eat-sleep-save-repeat. But note that, if anything, it’s even less plausible to say that in this situation you should just shrug your shoulders and say “whelp, guess I won’t save this child after all.” The number of children you should save is not as many as humanly possible—but it’s definitely not 0 either.

The tag bolted through her ear calls her G-2251. She squealed when they hole-punched her with it on her second day of life, and she’s worn it ever since.

G-2251 bites hard on metal. Forty million years of evolution have made her an intelligent, social forager, but she’s encased in a cage so tight that she can’t turn around. She has untreated wounds and ulcers. Her sense of smell (over a thousand times stronger than a human’s) is overwhelmed by the feces and dried blood that surround her. She’ll spend her life here.

G-2251 is pregnant. She scratches the empty floor helplessly, driven by an urge to build a nest for her children. She’ll raise them in a cage for ten days before they’re taken away and she’s inseminated again. Her sons will be castrated and have their tails removed without painkillers or anesthetic. Some of her daughters will move to crates of their own.3

This still leaves us in an uncomfortable situation: We should definitely do something but we probably don’t have to do as much as we possibly can, yet there’s no plausible line to draw between these two poles.

What makes this situation especially uncomfortable is that there is no solution. It’s simply not plausible to say that there’s any particular amount you have to do, after which everything else is extra credit. And even if there were, it’s hard to see how we could get any good justification for where it is. Instead you have to make up with yourself how much you want to do. You have to decide what you think is a reasonable amount of children to save.

Here’s something that seems reasonable to me: Giving away 10% of your income. If you do this, you can rest easy knowing that you will save several lives throughout your life. Were you to do that with your hands, you’d rightly be considered a hero—the difference is that you do it with your salary instead.

But while you’ll be making a heroic difference to the world, it’s not enough to meaningfully reduce your own quality of life. You’ll not be struggling to care for your own children because you’re pulling others’ out of ponds. If you live in a reasonably wealthy country—as you probably do if you’re reading this—the biggest hardship you’ll endure is foregoing some luxury goods that probably don’t improve your life much anyways. And in return you’ll know that you leave the world better than had you not entered it.

Naturally, 10% doesn’t have any deep significance, other than being a nice, round number. There’s some historical precedent with tithing and whatever, but apart from that it’s an arbitrary number, just like any other would be. If someone were to ask you why you don’t give 10.5% or 11% instead, there’s no good answer. But that’s true for any number other than 0% and as much as possible—but we already discussed those.

The Hiroshima chapter of The Making of the Atomic Bomb is the most horrifying thing I’ve ever read. I cried; my friend said it made him sick. Eyewitnesses saw “men whose whole bodies were covered with blood, and women whose skin hung from them like a kimono, plunged shrieking into the river” –I’ll stop there. But you should know that a nuclear weapon is probably pointed at your location right now.

Of course, the scale of death and suffering caused by nuclear weapons directly is nothing compared to the future they’d be throwing away. If a nuclear winter caused human extinction or irreversible collapse, trillions of lives would never get to feel love or joy. Even with conservative population estimates, extinction would mean eighty trillion people would never get to be born, outnumbering us ten thousand to one.

[…]

Hell could be a billion years of silence. It could be ~80,000,000,000,000 lives wiped away by one generation’s stupidity.4

Well, there is one way in which 10% is significant: It’s the number on the Giving What We Can 10% Pledge. If you think that you should pull the child out of the pond, I implore you to seriously consider taking this pledge.

By doing so, you in no way bind yourself legally. All you’re doing is making a good-faith promise that you will give at least 10% of what you earn from now on to whatever organizations you think can effectively make the world better. There are no rules for where to give, and no one will come after you if you fail.

You don’t have to give 10% of each paycheck you receive. If you are having a hard time at one point in your life, you can take a break and then compensate later—it’s important to be good to yourself.

From my own experience as a seasoned miser, there’s not any money-spending pain associated with letting some recurring donations run in the background of your life. And once you get used to your new income level, you hardly feel it. If anything, you only feel better knowing that you’re doing something to better the world without even lifting a finger.5

If you’re a student, there’s an option to give away 1% of your spending money until you get a real job. I think this is a good idea. You shouldn’t be self-flagellating when the sums you could currently give are not much in the scheme of your life anyways.6

Oh, and you also get a cool piece of paper:

It’s easy to become lost in the philosophical weeds, considering objections and counter-objections. Sometimes it’s healthy to take a step back and look at the issue with eyes as fresh as you can make them.

Remember how you felt reading those vignettes scattered throughout this post? If not, try to read one of them again.

Really imagine that it’s your son or mother suddenly wasting away in your arms—or you whose life is unexpectedly doomed to end before next Friday. Imagine that an animal with as much soul and personality as your dog is mutilated and locked up, never to see the sun again.

There are individuals for whom these stories are currently a hundred times more real than whatever you imagined.

Look out your window, and imagine the streets you walk every day empty. No soul to ever set foot in them again. No one ever giggling about a stupid inside joke that takes 5 years of friendship to find funny. No nose ever enjoying the smell of summer that you always forget until it returns on the first warm day.

Never before has this been a more serious possibility.

By giving to charities, you’re making a difference to these things. There will be fewer people and animals who have to suffer than if you had not given.7 It may not look as heroic as running into a burning building, but to the person that would have withered away from malaria, it matters just as much.

Giving away 10% of your income will of course not be enough. But that’s because nothing will ever be enough so long as there are still beings experiencing these things, and something left to do about it. However, it will be enough to do more good than most people in history have ever done—enough to make the world lucky to have had you.

If anyone takes the Giving What We Can Pledge in response to this article, I will give them a lifetime paid subscription to Wonder and Aporia. Just send me a DM (or even better, comment or restack).

Take the pledge

1

From ’s One Minute In Hell.

2

Well, as little as $3500 even.

3

From ’s One Minute In Hell.

4

From ’s One Minute In Hell.

5

Except when you set up the donation.

6

It also makes it very easy to reach quadruple-digit percentages of progress on the dashboard.

7

You may think this is doubtful, due to the complexity of these organizations and the causal chains. While I think it’s true that you can’t trace it back to any specific individual who would’ve died, were it not for you, it’s quite plausible that there will be more people alive than had you not donated. Especially if the charity is well-run and has room for more funding.

item.title: Harvesting Organs Is Wrong Because Blackmail Is Wrong
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Hello reader! I have set up a script that reads the entire browser history of any device that clicks on this post. That means that I now have all your dirty little secrets. All the depraved porn and (*shudders*) posts you’ve been consuming—it’s all mine.

And you know what? I'll release it! I swear I'll release it, so everyone can see what a sick little freak you are!

Unless, that is, you become a paid subscriber for the modest sum of $5. That's all.

—Yours Truly

Subscribe now

Supposing I’m being serious here, and planning on making good on my generous promise (which I am), is what I’m doing wrong? If the decision I’m blackmailing you into weren’t so prudent, we’d like to say yes: It’s wrong to blackmail people.

However, it’s hard to make sense of why that is. Let’s say I’m already going to release the information. When I blackmail you, all I’m doing is giving you an extra choice. If you value $5 less than your friends, family, and Wonder and Aporia posts, you’ll be better off than if I just released the whole, grim truth without asking. And if you value it more, then you don’t have to accept, and you lose nothing (other than the time spent thinking). Blackmail simply dominates not doing it.

Now, maybe there’s something a little sketchy about the way I acquired said information. But suppose I already got it, whether or not that was wrong, it’s surely wrong for me to then additionally blackmail you.

In fact, we can suppose that I’m a journalist, and you’re some big name in politics or whatever. As it happens, I’m sat behind you on the bus. I happen to glance over the seat, and find you sexting with your secretary (who is not your spouse (of which you have one)).1 Not only that, but stupid little me was unintentionally filming with my meta-glasses the whole time! “Whelp, now that I’ve got the footage, I might as well publish it” I think. However, after deciding on this, I get the even more brilliant idea of passing you a note that asks for a hefty sum in exchange for not publishing the video. Would that be wrong?

Again it seems so! But that’s very strange. The gathering of the evidence was not wrong, as it was all an accident. Furthermore, it’s unlikely to be wrong or illegal for me to publish the video, as it was filmed in a public place, and I, as a journalist, have a responsibility to bring this sort of news.2 And by blackmailing you, I’m only giving you more options.

Still it seems wrong! what’s going on?

I want to say that the action of blackmailing is not intrinsically wrong. But it’s still wrong in a very important sense—and it’s wrong in the same way that harvesting organs is wrong for utilitarians.

item.title: Moore Ado About Skepticism
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
1I am once again making and absolute fool of G.E. Moore and his supposed “proof” of an external world! Mwahahahaa!! You can all stop discussing this silly argument in your undergrad courses, philosophy journals, or wherever else you guys get off (philosophically speaking), and instead just read what I have to say and be done with it.

This was originally an exam essay. For this reason you will not be blessed with my characteristic quick wit and ever-ready hysterical remarks, which I know you all love and live for. As a tradeoff, the arguments will be much more sleek and sexy, giving you a lot more rigor-per-word (I quite like the diagnosis/arguments I give here).

1. Introduction

Here is one sentence. And here is another. There are at least two sentences here. Therefore there exists the beginning of an essay. Substitute in hands and you have a rigorous proof of an external world. Or so G.E. Moore claimed anyway (1939). The proof is supposed to refute external world skepticism, i.e. the idea that you cannot know that there is an external world as there appears to be, due to the possibility of being massively deceived. All but those with the least reflective of childhoods have surely felt the grip of the skeptical challenge at one point or another, and it would thus be a welcome surprise if it could be escaped simply by holding up your hands in succession. But despite the grand promise (or perhaps because of it), one is left with a feeling that something tricky is going on here. It cannot be that easy, right? No, say I! It really cannot, and Moore’s argument is no aid to us in the fight against skepticism. My claim is that the Moorean proof fails to succeed as a proof of an external world due to being justificatorily circular.

In §2 I lay out the skeptical challenge, and I present Moore’s proof in §3. The proof is diagnosed and deemed unsuccessful in §4. §5 is then devoted to anticipating and answering objections to my diagnosis—that it can be avoided with direct realism, that it can be avoided with liberalism about perception, and that a slightly different interpretation of Moore avoids it.

2. Here Is One Argument

Let us briefly lay out the skeptical challenge and some motivations for it, through giving a skeptical argument. First three clarifying definitions: I define “alternative to P” simply as a proposition that entails the falsity of P. A set of alternatives to P is said to be “relevant” just in case I should have a credence so high in their disjunction as to render P sufficiently improbable for knowledge. Finally I take evidence to mean positive relevance: E is evidence for H iff P(H|E) > P(H). P(A) is the probability of A and P(A|B) is the probability of A given B. The relevant probabilities here are subjective probabilities.

The first step of the argument consists in comparing the real world hypothesis (RWH)—that the world is roughly as it appears to you, with trees, hands, etc.—to some skeptical hypothesis (SH) that you are deceived into believing this without it being so. Consider the following hypothesis: You are a (handless) brain in a vat of fluid, connected via electrodes to a computer, stimulating you to have exactly the experiences you’re currently having. This and other SH’s, are both alternatives to P and (so goes the argument) jointly relevant. After all, you could have no evidence favoring RWH over SH, and you’re surely not justified in ruling SH out as irrelevant a priori—they are perfectly imaginable alternatives, and most people have been worried by them at one point or another.

The second step then goes that if you cannot rule out relevant alternatives, then you cannot know the RWH. After all—assuming knowledge is closed under entailment—if I know P and Q→¬P, then I can simply infer (and hence know) ¬Q. Thus if I do not know ¬Q that must mean that I do not know P. This may be bad enough in itself. But sticking with this closure principle, we can derive that for any ordinary proposition, O, that assumes RWH (such as that you have hands, or are currently sitting) you also do not know that. This gets us:

  1. (S does not know ¬SH)→(S does not know O).

  2. S does not know ¬SH.

  3. S does not know O.

3. But Here Is Another

Not a particularly pleasant conclusion. But in his Proof of an External World, G.E. Moore (1939) provides a quite simple proof to escape the problem:

By holding up my two hands, and saying, as I make a certain gesture with the right hand, ‘Here is one hand’, and adding, as I make a certain gesture with the left, ‘and here is another.’ (Ibid.)

From this he may deduce that two human hands exist at this moment. And since hands are external objects, it follows that there is an external world. We may formalize the argument as follows (Moore himself does not do this):

  1. Here is one hand.

  2. Here is another.

  3. Two hands exist at this moment.

  4. Therefore there exists an external world.

This, he takes it, is a perfectly rigorous proof—in fact, one could not ask for a better one. To corroborate, he lays out three criteria for successful proofs:

  1. The premises should be different than the conclusion.

  2. The premises must be known, not merely believed.

  3. The conclusion must follow from the premises.

(I) is clearly satisfied, as he might have hands or there might be an external world, whether or not there is one hand here and now. And nothing could be more plain than that (II) is satisfied, Moore claims. In denying it, “[y]ou might as well suggest that I do not know that I am now standing up and talking” (ibid.). While not in a strictly valid form as stated, (III) can certainly be allowed, given that we are not overly pedantic—and crucially given that “hand” is interpreted as “a hand in the external world” rather than “the appearance as of a hand.” Hence all boxes are checked.

I shall first take the straightforward interpretation that Moore is simply presenting the above syllogism as a direct proof of an external world (and by implication against any skeptical hypothesis). This seems to be the interpretation in e.g. (Pritchard, 2007) and (Pryor, 2004). A slightly different interpretation is presented in §5.3.

4. Diagnosing the Proof

I do not believe this proof is successful. To lay out the case, I will first consider what the role of a proof is, and what it takes for one to be successful. One important distinction regards the scope of the proof:

Firstly it may function to persuade a (hypothetical) interlocutor who is not already convinced of the position in question. If this is the intent of Moore’s proof, I believe it immediately fails its purpose. After all, any skeptic will simply deny that we know that any hands exist in the first place—by raising his fists, Moore is bringing no new consideration to the table that the skeptic would not already have considered.

Secondly the proof might function to justify one’s own belief in a position. That is, we are persuading no one other than ourselves, and simply making salient reasons for why we may hold the beliefs we do. I take it that this is a much more plausible interpretation of what Moore’s argument is trying to achieve.

We ought also consider what a proof should be a proof against. Specifically, a proof should rule out all relevant alternatives to its conclusion, though it may plausibly leave irrelevant alternatives untouched. That there are at least two apples on a table can be easily proven by looking: Here is one apple, and here is another, so there are at least two apples on the table. But suppose I remember having many fake plastic apples in the house. This raises the relevant alternative that what I see are simply plastic replicas. The above proof would no longer work as there is now a relevant alternative it does not rule out. This may appear to be a contextualist point, but it need not be (and I do not wish it to be). After all, I might hold that “relevant” does not vary contextually in meaning, and that it is simply the justification for my credences that has changed.

Should we then simply add a further criterion to Moore’s three that a proof should rule out all relevant alternatives? That would not work, as any valid proof really does rule out all inconsistent possibilities, simply in virtue of its logical form; from “here are two apples” it really does follow that “there are at least two apples on the table.” Instead I propose the criterion:

  1. The inference is not justificatorily circular against any relevant set of alternatives to the conclusion.

Let us expand on what is meant by “justificatory circularity”:

The inference from premises P to the falsity of alternative A is justificatorily circular IFF P is not immediately known AND for all my evidence E to justify P(P)=X, I must presuppose that P(¬A)≥X.

This will take some unpacking. The first conjunct ensures that the P in question does in fact rely on some evidence (more on this in §5.1). The general idea of “presupposing” is that an inference from E to P presupposes Q just in case a belief in Q is “logically prior” to E justifying P. A way of illustrating this is to imagine yourself behind a sort of “veil of ignorance,” not knowing whether E obtains or not. For the inference from E to P(P)=X to presuppose P(Q)=Y then means that P(P|E)=X only if P(Q)=Y.

That is, even before finding out whether E, I have to already have P(Q)=Y to make the inference. Or applying it to justificatory circularity: Even before finding out whether E, I already hold ¬A to be at least as probable as the premises, which are supposed to establish ¬A.

It should be quite clear, then, that if E supporting P(P)=X presupposes P(¬A)≥X that is a problem for the proof in question. After all, the proof was supposed to show us that we need not worry about A. But if the premises being probable enough to show that we need not worry about A already presupposes that A is sufficiently improbable, then the proof cannot possibly serve its function. It might very well be that we really can be sure of ¬A, but we certainly do not have the proof in question to thank for it!

What does it take for some premises to make this presupposition? It essentially just requires that none of my evidence favors P over A. If some evidence favors P, then I could presuppose a credence in both P and ¬A less than X, and infer from the evidence to P(P)=X; and if no evidence favors P, then, well, I cannot do that.

We can now look at some examples which the keen reader may recognize, and see whether or not they satisfy criterion (IV). First imagine that I wish to prove that there at least two apples on my table, and that I have no particular reason to expect to see non-apple apple-like objects on my table—meaning (let us suppose) that no relevant alternatives involve me seeing non-apple apple-like objects on my table. As it happens, I see what appears to be two apples on my table, prompting me to give the following proof:

  1. Here is one apple.

  2. Here is another.

  3. There are at least two apples on my table.

This seems perfectly legitimate, and that is also the verdict (IV) gives. Ex hypothesi none of my relevant alternatives involve deceptive possibilities, including only things like “there is only one apple-like object on my table, which is an apple.” My evidence for believing (1) and (2)—i.e. my visual experience—thus does not presuppose that the disjunction of these is highly improbable. In fact I might antecedently be quite confident that there are no apples on the table, but since no relevant amount of my confidence here is in a “skeptical” possibility, it is easily overcome by my seeing what looks like two apples.

Suppose now that I have many plastic apples in my home, meaning some of my relevant alternatives involve non-apple apple-like objects on my table. Again I see what appears to be two apples, and produce the same proof as above.

Here things have clearly gone awry! The problem: My evidence does not adjudicate between (1) and (2), and the relevant alternatives to my conclusion, seeing as some relevant alternatives involve there being at least two apple-like objects on the table, which I would of course equally take to justify (1) and (2).

I am now troubled by the possibility that I might be a brain in a vat. To clear my mind of these doubts, I raise my hands and whisper to myself:

  1. Here is one hand.

  2. Here is another.

  3. Two hands exist at this moment.

  4. Therefore there exists an external world.

Did I succeed? Sadly, it seems not. The trouble is again that some of the relevant alternatives to my conclusion—such as my being a brain in a vat—predict my evidence equally as well as my premises. This means that the argument fails condition (IV). Remember why this is a problem: The trouble is that this means that I can only establish my premises to the extent that I presuppose that relevant alternatives are false. Thus I cannot possibly use this to rid myself of relevant alternatives.

It is of course very much possible that I should have a very high credence in (1) and (2), and be very confident that RWH is true. But the skeptical argument runs on the—quite plausible—idea that we may not start out assuming that skeptical alternatives are irrelevant, and so we cannot just start off assuming knowledge of (1) or (2). In any case it will have been through no fault of the Moorean argument if we end up knowing RWH.

5. Objections

I anticipate that the Moorean sympathizer will not yet be persuaded. Let me thus preempt some objections I suspect they might raise.

5.1. Direct Realism

Remember that an argument cannot fail (IV) if the premises are immediately known. In assuming that they aren’t, I appear to have been making the controversial assumption that direct realism—the view that objects in the external world are the immediate objects of (veridical) perception—is false. By the time of Proof of an External World, Moore himself was no longer a direct realist, it seems, favoring some sort of sense-data view (Moore, 1925, Section 4). Although John Greco (2002, p. 557) argues that Moore’s views are not incompatible with direct realism (or some position relevantly similar for our purposes), due to what he means by “sense-datum” (see e.g. (Moore, 1952, p. 643)). At any rate, our goal is not to perform flawless Moore-exegesis, but to consider what might be said in favor of his arguments (or arguments close enough).

If direct realism is true, I am immediately aware of my hands. My justification for the premises in Moore’s argument is then not some kind of inference from intermediary representations, but rather I just know that they are true—they are part of my immediate evidence.

However, this solution is cold comfort for my skeptical doubts. It only works given that I am in fact perceiving hands right now. But what I care about is not per se whether I technically know that I have hands; rather I care about whether I may be quite confident that I have hands, and this the direct realist solution doesn’t help me with. For when I look at what I take to be hands, I have no way of telling whether I am veridically perceiving or simply hallucinating hands. Direct realists—at least of a contemporary sort—will likely reject the idea that a veridical perception is the same kind of experience as a hallucination. But whether or not they are different kinds or not does not help ease my mind one bit, as they are completely indistinguishable to me either way.

I of course admit that I am relying on internalist intuitions here, and someone who is already sympathetic to epistemic externalism is unlikely to be moved here. However, if one does not feel the pull of the internalist intuitions here, one is unlikely to feel the pull of the skeptical challenge anyhow, as it is a non-problem to begin with for (many) externalists. At least if it is a non-problem—if I am a brain in a vat, skepticism is a problem. The direct realist response is of course not reliant on internalism, as one can claim that veridical perceptions are internal states. Nevertheless, the intuitions that make internalism compelling should make this response uncompelling.

5.2. Liberalism About Perception

A similar objection to this sort of diagnosis is raised by James Pryor (2004). He claims that we should be liberal, rather than conservative, regarding perceptual knowledge.

Let P be what my perceptual experiences are as of (e.g. that I have hands), and H be some hypothesis (e.g. that I perceive veridically). Conservatism then claims that for my perceptual experience to give me prima facie justification for P, I must have antecedent justification for H, whereas liberalism denies this. The idea is then that if we are liberals, we no longer need to presuppose P(¬A)≥X to end with P(P)=X, as we can get our justification for P without first consulting the status of A (¬A is our H in this case), even when A is an SH. I do not think this maneuver works though.

I take it that prima facie justification for P from your perceptual experiences is simply justification to hold a higher P(P) (by some amount) than you otherwise would have. The question is then whether getting this requires also having justification for ¬A. Even giving the negative (i.e. liberal) answer, does not avoid the diagnosis.

Imagine that you are behind a “veil of perceptive ignorance.” In this position, you have credences such that P(¬A)≥X and P(P)<X, and, for some experiences E, you would be justified in assigning P(P|E)=X. Recall, this is a paradigm illustration of presupposition. In other words you presuppose that the skeptical alternative is false with an equal or higher probability than X, but having E would justifiably raise your credence in P.

The veil is lifted, and—lo and behold!—you have E. This justifies assigning P(P)=X, and thus gives you prima facie justification for P. At the same time you have no specific justification for ¬A—or at least you’re not required to have that. Hence liberalism is satisfied. But had you presupposed P(¬A)<X, E would have to in some way favor P over A, in order to end up with P(P|E)=X. But when A is an SH, E is ex hypothesi no more surprising on A than on P, so it surely cannot favor P over A.

That is to say, you get prima facie justification for P without having direct justification for rejecting the SH (i.e. liberalism), but this does not help disprove the SH, as you still have to assume that P(¬A)≥X. So liberalism does not avoid the diagnosis.

Or perhaps I am misunderstanding liberalism, taking it to be weaker than it is. Perhaps the idea is that there is some quality to having the perceptual experience itself which adds to your justification, beyond the evidential value. In that case this may instead be considered an intuition pump against liberalism: Surely(! table slammed and foot stomped) there is no such quality! We can suppose that you had a perfectly vivid imagination behind the veil, being able to imagine exactly what it would be like to have these perceptual experiences; the only thing that happens is that you then actually have the experience. Are we supposed to believe that that adds some justification into the mix that you could not predict beforehand? I of course admit that I am again relying on internalist intuitions; read §5.1 for my response to that charge.

Or perhaps the point is that you get evidence favoring P over A from your perceptual experiences. This seems to imply one of three options:

  1. The liberal has not understood the skeptical hypothesis: The skeptical hypothesis by definition predicts all your evidence equally as well as P (assuming direct realism is false—and even then we saw even that was not quite enough).

  2. The liberal is using “evidence” differently than me: I use “evidence” to mean positive relevance. In fact, let me stipulate that to be what I mean! We are then talking past each other, but simply using words differently does not affect the substance of the issue in any way.

  3. The liberal is denying that our credences should conform with standard probability theory: Given a positive relevance definition of evidence, it simply follows from the Kolmogorov axioms that two hypotheses predicting something equally well means that it is not evidence favoring either. This is certainly not an impossible position to hold, but I believe it makes liberalism look less modest than initially expected.

5.3. Plausibility Comparison

Finally, William G. Lycan (2001) gives a reconstruction of Moore’s argument that ostensibly avoids my criticisms. Rather than the point being to give a straightforward proof of an external world, it is simply to invite a comparison of plausibility. The skeptic gives the modus ponens:

  1. (S does not know ¬SH)→(S does not know P).

  2. S does not know ¬SH.

  3. S does not know P.

And Moore gives us the corresponding modus tollens:

  1. (S does not know ¬SH)→(S does not know P).

  2. S knows P.

  3. S knows ¬SH.

But rather than simply asserting the latter argument, he asks us to consider which is more plausible. Or more specifically: Is (2) or (5) more plausible? And the idea is then that (5) is obviously going to be more plausible when O is something like “here is a hand.” Formulated this way, my charge of justificatory circularity does not stick, as the argument does not even have the requisite structure: It is not a deductive proof, but simply a comparison of plausibility.

While the exact diagnosis from before no longer works, I think a closely related one will. To see this, we must consider when we may compare plausibility, and when we may not. It is often perfectly legitimate to make this comparison. Consider:

You return home from work, and see two apples on your table. As you are admiring them, your partner, N.N., who left for work after you, calls you and (in an odd choice of conversation-topic) tells you “the table had no apples on it when I left, so there aren’t any on it now.” Even more inexplicably, they give you the following syllogism over the phone (pronouns substituted):

  1. If what N.N. tells you is true, there are no apples on the table.

  2. What N.N. tells you is true.

  3. Therefore there are no apples on the table.

But being a devout Moorean, you immediately reply:

  1. If what N.N. tells you is true, there are no apples on the table.

  2. There are apples on the table.

  3. Therefore what N.N. tells you is false.

You then compare (2) and (5), and find that (5) is much more plausible, meaning you make the corresponding inference. Everything looks fine here.

However, imagine you are again admiring some (apparent) apples, when N.N. calls you and tells you they have replaced all apples in the house with plastic replicas. This prompts you both to exchange the above arguments. Again you compare the premises and find (5) much more plausible than (2)—I mean, just look! There are obviously two apples there! This time something feels a little more off.

What went wrong? The trouble, it seems to me, is that in the second scenario, it is equally likely that you would find (5) more plausible than (2), regardless of which is actually the case. In the first scenario, if (2) is true, then it would be very unlikely that you would find (5) plausible. After all, if (2) were true, you probably would not seem to see two apples. There are naturally certain possibilities compatible with (2) where you would still find (5) as plausible (e.g. that you are hallucinating two apples), but these are not probable enough to be relevant, simply given (2). In the second scenario, it is basically just as likely that you would find (5) most plausible, either way, since (2) being the case predicts you finding (5) very plausible equally well.

Why is this problematic, then? Well, I think it should be quite clear: Your confidence in the premises in no way tracks their truth. While you do not use your confidence as evidence for the premise, meaning the problem is not underdetermination of evidence, you still seem to have a higher-order defeater for your belief. After all, if all of your mental states (including the reasons you cite for your confidence) are equally predicted by two hypotheses, trusting your reasons for favoring one over the other seems to be pure dogmatism!

6. Conclusion

I thus stand by my initial thesis: The Moorean proof fails to succeed as a proof of an external world due to being justificatorily circular. Justificatory circularity, of course, in the sense I defined in §4, and which I defended as being a necessary criterion for a successful proof. Further, I claim that neither direct realism, liberalism, or a reinterpretation of Moore’s argument saves it from succumbing to this problem (or some equally troublesome related problem as in §5.3).

This is not to say that skepticism is an unsolvable problem. Far from it! I believe something like an abductivist or bayesian response might, for example, very well be successful. What it is to say is that the Moorean proof is doing no work here, and to the extent that it is sound, it is simply due to being parasitic on another solution. If some other response is successful, that might also very well explain why the Moorean proof has quite some intuitive appeal—we really are justified in rejecting skepticism, and so Moore’s proof really does go through in some (pedantic) sense. Nevertheless, it still fails qua proof, as it does not help alleviate the skeptical worry in any way.

item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
This is a translation of a project I did on the question of why vegans are hated. Unlike what I usually do, this was undertaken with the help of a lot of Continental theory. So if you are otherwise skeptical of the merit of continental philosophy, this may also be a fun project.

The project had to include empirical investigation (*ugh*) so it is based on a number of interviews (which I have of course made GDPR-kosher). All in all it turned out a lot more interesting than I expected, and I think there were some interesting insights to be had.

1. Introduction

Vegetarians and vegans are a hated group. According to one study, vegans are viewed as negatively as immigrants and feminists, and more negatively than environmental activists (MacInnis & Hodson, 2017). Shared meals in particular are a battleground for negative interactions (Salmivaara et al., 2022). It is not immediately obvious why vegetarianism and veganism are viewed so negatively—and especially why they are viewed more negatively than seemingly comparable movements such as climate movements.

In this article, I will therefore investigate where the negative view of vegetarians and vegans comes from—especially in relation to meals. More precisely, I will examine the issue: How do the unique social structures of the meal affect the negative view of vegetarians and vegans, and the conflicts vegetarian and vegan lifestyles give rise to? The issue is examined through semi-structured interviews and theories from Harré and Van Langenhove, Simmel, Douglas, Gadamer and Habermas.

The article proceeds as follows: §2 explains positioning theory (theoretical and methodological framework). §3 reviews empirical method. §4 presents Simmel and Douglas, which are used in §5. §6 adds Gadamer and Habermas, leading to analysis in §7. §8 discusses options for improving meals with vegetarians, before §9 concludes that the conflict stems from three interwoven relationships: the grammar of the meal, its balance between individuality and community, and a clash between two different normative horizons.1

item.title: Should the Numbers (of Hours) Count?
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Tohn M. Jaurek is at the dentists office signing a waiver. Despite the dentists’ strongly worded advice, Tohn insists on not being anesthetized during his tooth extraction, as he’ll be able to save $5 on materials. After incessant pestering, the staff relented, so long as Tohn was willing to sign a waiver. Fine with him!

Just as he’s about to put the pen to the page, a flash of light illuminates the room. Before Tohn M. Jaurek stands… a wrinkly Tohn M. Jaurek?

Jaurek [the Tohn M. Jaurek who just popped into the room]: STOP IT! You don’t know what you’re gett—

Tohn [the Tohn M. Jaurek about to sign a waiver]: Woah there! Calm down a second. What the hell just happened? Why am I… you… we here?

Jaurek: Oh yeah, sorry. I’m you from the future. I know, it’s a little cliché, but I couldn’t think of anything better.

Tohn: I’ll let it slide.

Jaurek: I’ve come here to warn you that what you’re about to do is a huge mistake!

Tohn: I don’t think it’s possible for you to change that. Actually, you’re probably not even really me.

Jaurek: Wow, I must be fun at parties… If you’re that pedantic, the author has a footnote for you.1

Tohn: Okay fine. But what are you doing here?

Jaurek: Well, after you sign that waiver, you’ll have your tooth pulled out without anesthetic. The pain is completely intolerable, and you’re left traumatized. Literally the worst decision of your entire life. As a result you—by which I mean I—invent a time machine, through sheer determination, to correct your past mistake, which leads me here.

Tohn: Oh, that’s all? When then you can go back where you came from.

Tohn grabs the pen again, about to sign the waiver. Jaurek leaps forward and grabs his hand.

Jaurek: ARE YOU CRAZY?! Did you not hear what I said?

Tohn: Loud and clear.

Jaurek: The pain is unbearable! You’re willing to go through this torment for $5?? I’ll give you $5 right now if it’s that.

Jaurek pulls out a crisp $5 note from 2066

Jaurek: Uhh… Nevermind, you probably can’t legally use that.

Tohn: And the pain of the needle.

Jaurek: Excuse me?

Tohn: You said I do it for the $5. I also do it to avoid the pain of the needle that they give the anesthesia with.

Jaurek: What difference does that make? The pain of the extraction is obviously worse than that!

Tohn: Is it really? I did some research before coming here. Turns out that there is a split second where the stab of the needle is just as painful as anything that happens throughout the rest of the procedure.2

Jaurek: Okay? But the procedure is much longer than a split second. You barely register the needle—but I don’t think you can comprehend just how horrible the procedure is.

Tohn: Yeah I know. But I just don’t really care about that part.

Jaurek: Well, I think you should! It’s clearly worse.

Tohn: Look at it like this: Suppose you’re given the choice between saving your peripheral friend Dave from the pain of the needle vs. saving a stranger from the pain of the procedure. It seems reasonable that it’d be permissible to save Dave.

Jaurek: What? No it doesn’t!

Tohn: Oh okay then, scrap that. Then what about this: When you’re saying that it’s worse, who is it worse for?

Jaurek: Me—that is, you.

Tohn: And what is this “you”?

Jaurek: What do you mean?

Tohn: Well, here we are, talking to each other. Each of us is supposedly “me.” But we have entirely different thoughts, feelings, values, and so on. If I kick you in the balls, I won’t feel a thing.

Jaurek: Sure you will. Just not yet.

Tohn: I guess by some definition of the word, yeah. But is that really a sense that matters? I won’t feel it now. So if I just don’t care, why does it matter if I’m technically the same person as you.

Jaurek: Are you really dragging us down into the metaphysical mud of personal identity, just to save $5?

Tohn: I’m not meaning to do that! Say what you will about personal identity—what I say is independent of that. Now, what can you say to me if I just don’t care about how my future time slices feel?

Jaurek: I’ll say that it’s bad for you! Whether or not you care, it’ll be bad for you.

Tohn: But will it be bad for me-now or me-in-the-future?

Jaurek: You-in-the-future, but that’s still the same person.

Tohn: In what important sense is it, though? What is this person-entity you’re talking about? Maybe it’s true as a matter of metaphysics that I am that future person. But there’s no state of awareness that’s thinking about what to say right now and is also feeling that pain.

Jaurek: Er, I mean, I guess not. You’re not having both experiences at the same time.

Tohn: Right, so if I don’t care about the suffering of me-in-the-future, what mistake am I making? What difference is there between me-in-the-future and some random other person similar to me?

Jaurek: The difference surely is that you can anticipate and fear your future suffering in a way you wouldn’t anticipate others’ suffering.

Tohn: But is that not just a contingent matter of my psychology? I anticipate it because I-now really care about my future self in a very special way. However, couldn’t I happen to be constituted so that I didn’t. Just like someone could be constituted in a weird way where they don’t care about the suffering of their close family members. As I said, there’s no consciousness of both me-now and the future pain—there is no entity experiencing both in any important sense.

Jaurek: I feel like you’re assuming a deflationary view of personhood now, even though you said you wouldn’t talk about metaphysics. If I really am, in some deep sense, the same person over time, then surely I’d be irrational to have this strange psychology, in a way that having the same attitude regarding other people isn’t.

Tohn: I am not. Consider whether it is likewise irrational to not care about other people. To settle this question, it wouldn’t matter whether we settle the metaphysics of whether you’re part of this entity called a “group” or not.

Jaurek: Maybe not.

Tohn: But it sounds like you want to have it both ways: There’s something special about the intrapersonal case that’s not there for the interpersonal case. I have to care specially about my own future in a way that I don’t have to care about other people.

Jaurek: Right.

Tohn: But compare these three positions: 1) It’s rational to pursue whatever you care about right now, 2) it’s irrational to pursue a smaller benefit for me now over a greater benefit for me later, and 3) it’s irrational to pursue a smaller benefit for me over a greater benefit for others. You’re trying to say that (2) is specially plausible in a way that (3) is not.

Jaurek: Yes, that’s right.

Tohn: But that’s an unstable position! When I choose what to do, I choose now. Other people differ in the I, and my later selves—like you—differ in the now. In both cases, the thing that’s actually choosing is differentiated, either through time or person. If you want to appeal to stuff like that my future experiences will be painful or whatnot, that doesn’t get you anywhere, since other people’s experiences are also painful.

Jaurek: But there is a difference: The future pain is mine.

Tohn: Right, but before we agreed that the metaphysics of groups didn’t matter. If it happens that there’s some deep metaphysical sense in which I’m part of a group, so that another person’s pain is the group’s as much as mine, that doesn’t matter. The metaphysics is irrelevant here. Likewise, if it turns out that your pain is mine in some deep metaphysical sense, that doesn’t really matter. In each case I’m the thing that’s choosing, and the mere fact that there’s this wider entity I’m a part of doesn’t do anything by itself. You’d need to give me further reasons to care about the larger entity. And as soon as you try to do that, the arguments cut both ways—treating the intrapersonal case inherently differently from the interpersonal case is unjustifiable.

Jaurek: Okay, fine, maybe I should be an altruist then. And maybe you are consistent in your position. You can’t convince the consistent skeptic, and you can’t convince the consistent present-aim egoist. But I can still charge you of being immoral—of not taking your future selves into account. Don’t you care about morality?

Tohn: Sure I do. But maybe I didn’t make it clear enough what I’m arguing. What I’m arguing is a moral conclusion, not a self-interest based one. The symmetry with intrapersonal and interpersonal self-interest is just an important step. I’m not just arguing that I’m not inconsistent if I don’t care, but that it’s literally not worse if I have my tooth extracted without anesthetic. I don’t have any inherent reason to prefer the needle over the procedure.

Jaurek: You can’t be serious.

Tohn: Deeply serious. When you say that some option is “worse,” what do you mean? What makes it worse?

Jaurek: That someone is experiencing extra pain or something.

Tohn: Right, so it’d be fair to say that it’s because it’s worse for someone?

Jaurek: I guess so.

Tohn: Aha! Well with this surgery, who is it worse for?

Jaurek: For the you during the surgery.

Tohn: Is it really though? Let’s call the time-slice at the time of the needle prick T1 and the set of time-slices during the surgery T2 to T1000. So we’re supposing that there are 999 slices during the surgery. Now, you might think that the surgery is 999 times worse. But it’s not 999 times worse for any slice, is it? If I choose the anesthetic, it’s worse for T1 and if I don’t choose it, it’s worse for T2 to T1000.

Jaurek: Sure, it’s not worse for any particular time-slice, but it’s worse for the whole aggregate.

Tohn: And what is this “aggregate” you’re talking about? As we just established, there’s no unified experience of the whole set. So I ask you again: You say that it’s worse to not take the anesthetic. But worse for who?

Just as Tohn finishes his sentence, the two interlocutors are blinded by another flash.

M. [the even wrinklier Tohn M. Jaurek who just popped into the room]: STOP IT! You don’t know what you’re gett—

M. looks at Jaurek.

M.: Who are you?

Jaurek: I’m here to convince my old self not to go through this tooth extraction without anesthetic.

M.: Weird, me too. I guess you must have failed.

Jaurek: Wouldn’t you remember that.

M.: I don’t know. I’ve been getting a little senile lately, so maybe I forgot. But the memories of that procedure have still been haunting me into my old age. Then one day I found a box labeled “Time Machine” in the garage. I didn’t remember where it came from, but I decided to try and

Jaurek: Yeah, well I hope you’ll have more luck than I did. We were denser back then than I remember.

Jaurek recounts the dialectic up until this point.

M.: What, is this guy insane?

Jaurek: I can’t rule it out.

Tohn: Guys, can we cut the crap? I’m not paying for that anesthetic.

M.: Maybe you’ll change your mind after this. Up until now you were not convinced that not getting anesthetic was worse, when you just knew that it was this guy [pointing at Jaurek] who’d suffer.

Tohn: Right.

M.: But now that you know that I’ve been suffering too, you should accept that not getting anesthetic is worse.

Tohn: I don’t see why?

M.: Let’s call the set time slices that only I, and not Jaurek, have experienced TM. Before you knew whether TM had suffering, you said that neither option was worse than the other. But TM having suffering is worse for the members of TM. So adding the suffering of TM is worse for some and better for no one—and so it’s surely worse overall. So if neither option were worse than the other at first, then making one option worse should surely make that option worse than the other. Now you can’t ask “worse for who?” The answer is: “Worse for me.”

Tohn: You’re assuming that badness works in a simplistic way where adding some to one side can break a tie—that it’s fungible in some way. But that’s exactly what I’m rejecting! I said that not getting the anesthesia is “not worse” than getting it, not that it’s “as bad.”

M.: What, so you’re rejecting the transitivity of badness? That’s got to be the craziest thing you’ve said so far!

Tohn: Well, it’s only crazy if you accept the fungibility you’re assuming. When I say that neither option is worse, I’m saying that they have a sort of “parity” but they’re also in a sense incomparable. In that case it’s not at all crazy to say that transitivity doesn’t hold—you don’t get the sorts of preference loops that you otherwise run into.3

M. [Sighs]: I’m too old for this...

The room lights up again, and when their eyes readjust, Tohn and Jaurek yet again find themselves alone in the room.

Tohn: So much for that, I guess.

Jaurek: Seems I didn’t grow anymore patient with old age. Well, I don’t need that guy anyways! What he said gave me a thought: I think you’re failing to account for equality. Surely you agree that equality is important?

Tohn: It certainly depends what you mean! I don’t care about all time-slices having exactly the same welfare.

Jaurek: No, what I mean is more fundamental: That each time-slice has equal moral weight. That is, each time-slice counts for one and only one.

Tohn: Sure, that seems right. But how am I in conflict with that?

Jaurek: Well, you’re treating some of your time-slices as privileged. Specifically, you’re putting a lot more weight on the time slice that will experience the needle, vs. the time-slices that will undergo the horror of the operation. If each counted for one, the interests of the many would obviously outweigh the interests of the few—that is, more would count for more.

Tohn: Nope, equality doesn’t get you there! I’ll just steal an argument from this philosopher called who claims to have graduated from MIT. He wrote a paper about some guy called John M. Taurek.

Jaurek: Strange name.

Tohn: Yeah it’s a little weird. But no connection. Anyways, I’ll retrofit the important things from this Muñoz-character’s article to what we’re talking about here. The key is to treat our decisions like voting systems.

Jaurek: Why would we do that?

Tohn: Well, it lets us be more precise about what exactly we mean with “equality.” So let’s say that we’re voting over actions, and each time-slice gets a “vote” depending on whether some action is good or bad for it. Our theory of aggregation (or lack thereof) is then our voting rule, and the verdict is over which action to choose.

Jaurek: I’m following.

Tohn: Now, we can then express equality in terms of constraints on our voting rule. Specifically, equality seems to come down to anonymity: That who casts each vote doesn’t matter. The fact that some time-slice is this time-slice doesn’t matter when counting up the vote.

Jaurek: But you’re clearly violating that when you favor the earlier time-slice!

Tohn: Not quite. You can see my view as “unanimity rule.” Every time-slice has to agree on some action for it to be deemed correct. Otherwise we just have a tie. And so I can choose to skip the anesthetic if I want the $5 instead. It’s not because it’s this time-slice that objects, but because there’s some that does—and so I also have anonymity.

Jaurek: Right well clearly there’s something wrong with having anonymity be the only criterion for equality. It’s not just enough that no one is special—but everyone has to count for something. Specifically we could say that if we have a tie, adding one more vote on one side should turn the result in that direction. As we saw when M. was still among us, that’s clearly not something you can get.

Tohn: I simply reject that that’s a requirement. Every slice is perfectly equal with unanimity rule. Slices don’t always have to be able to make a difference to count as equal—in fact they don’t even do that for you. If we have anything else than a tie, no one can make a difference. I just set the threshold in a stricter place. But it’s not less equal for that reason. To be frank, I think trying to give an argument to convince me from neutral premises is a fool’s errand.

The two Tohn M. Jaureks fall silent. Jaurek seems to finally have run out of things to say. Maybe Tohn was right all along? But just as Tohn is about to reach for the pen again…

KNOCK KNOCK KNOCK

…

A dentist pops her head in the door.

Dentist: What the hell is taking you so lo—

She rubs her eyes, takes a deep breath, and looks at Tohn M. Jaurek. Then at Tohn M. Jaurek, and finally back at Tohn M. Jaurek. Then she decides that after Tohn’s ludicrous wishes, this is not the strangest thing she’s experienced today.

Dentist: [Sigh] Look, you’re really cutting it close with the time here. Also, there’s another guy who just came in needing an emergency root canal, who’ll need to be treated after you. If you insist on being difficult about this and not taking the anesthetic, your extraction will take longer, and he’ll have to sit there and suffer even more. Just sayin’.

Tohn: Great, I’ll be there in a sec!

The dentist shakes her head and shuts the door.

Jaurek: So you’re gonna get the anesthetic now, right?

Tohn: What, why would I do that?

Jaurek: Are you kidding me?! You’re just gonna let some poor guy suffer so that you can save 5 bucks?

Tohn: I mean, it’s not any worse—so why would I not?

Jaurek: Jesus Christ! You’ve been going on and on about “oh, worse for who?,” but clearly the aggregationist respects what’s worse for people at least as well as you do. Let’s grant that the equality argument doesn’t go through. Well, then your argument about aggregation requiring some “impersonal good” certainly doesn’t entail your innumerate ethics either!

Tohn: And why is that?

Jaurek: I mean, just consider the voting analogy. Each of us is equally counting up votes—you just stop after one. But it’s not that I have some “super-vote” that the other votes are transformed into. I’m simply counting individual votes.

Tohn: But you’re still counting them, right? In other words, you’re treating them as fungible goods that can be measured with a single parameter. What you’re making your decision on the basis of is this abstract value, rather than the plights of individual slices.

Jaurek: Oh, but I am not! Just think of M. back there. The reason that adding his pain into consideration tipped the scales was because of his pain—not because it made some number go up. Worse for who? Worse for M.

Tohn: But you still need the abstract aggregated pain to even be able to make your decision.

Jaurek: I can represent the decision with some number, yes. But I can likewise represent your theory with some abstract thing: You’re simply making decisions on the basis of some abstract comparator that checks to see whether someone will be harmed on each option, and either outputs “indifferent” or “option X is better.” That’s no less abstract or objectionable than the aggregationist picture—only yours ignores more information. The fault is of course that even though these representations are equivalent to the corresponding decision rules, they’re not what we actually care about. The reason I care about the aggregate is because I care about each of the people it’s an aggregate of. And the reason you care about the comparator is… Well I don’t really get it, to be honest.

Tohn: But you’re still making decisions based on some overall impersonal “worse” rather than “worse for.” Maybe we can represent each view abstractly, but you’re committed to using an abstracted impersonal value, whereas I can get away with just looking to individual time-slices by themselves.

Jaurek: I don’t see how I am committed to that anymore than you are. I can just make pairwise comparisons. I can see that T1 will be in pain if you get the anesthetic, and that T2 will be in pain if you don’t, so these have equal claims. I can then notice that T3 will also be in pain if you don’t get the anesthetic, and so there’s more “worse for” on one side. And I can maybe weight these comparisons by the degree of pain, and so on. None of this requires reference to some impersonal “worse.” It’s all just “worse for.”

Tohn: But you’re smuggling in the impersonal worse when you’re tallying up the weights on each side.

Jaurek: Well, you’re also tallying up on each side. It’s just that you can only count to one. If the problem is keeping track of who we’ve counted and who we haven’t, then we’re both in trouble. And if neither of us can make neutral arguments, we would have to go with the view that’s most reasonable on the face of it. Given the insanity of what you’re signing up for right now, I think it’s a pretty open and shut case.

Tohn furrows his brows for a moment, before looking back to Jaurek.

Tohn: Alright, so let's call it a draw.

Jaurek: What? No! If your argument is right, then you have no more reason to choose one over the other. But if I’m right, you have decisive reason to choose the anesthesia. So surely you should choose the anesthesia when we're in a stalemate like this!

Tohn: Oh, so you want to discuss moral uncertainty too? I'm game.

Jaurek—like M.—decides that arguing with this maniac of a past self is even worse than the torture of the procedure, and elects to cut his losses. So Tohn finally signs the waiver, and the tooth extraction begins. Naturally he immediately regrets his choice. But the Tohn of 5 minutes ago regrets nothing.

If you don’t subscribe I’ll find you and pull your teeth out with no anesthetic.

item.title: Job Loss Is Not Bad
item.description: At least not for the reasons you think
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Whenever any policy of any sort is discussed, there’ll inevitably be an outcry from some group about how this destroys jobs. Climate regulation? That will destroy jobs in sectors relying on fossil fuels. Self-driving cars? That will put an end to taxi drivers. And—most infuriating—animal welfare regulations? Farmers will be put out of business. Oh the horror!

This pattern of argument is very frustrating! It usually reflects a naive view of the world, where you can never step on anyone’s toes to make the world a better place. Now, it’s not necessarily that loss is never bad. As we will see, there are ways in which job loss definitely can be bad. The problem is that the focus is usually on some decidedly unimportant aspects.

What is job loss?

When someone says that policy X will cause job loss, this is ambiguous between two claims:

  1. Policy X will cause some people to lose their jobs, and

  2. Policy X will decrease overall employment.

(2) is a much stronger claim than (1), but it’s also the one that would drive most of the harm of job loss.

If all that happens is (1), then some people will lose their jobs, yes, but that will be balanced out by some other people (or maybe the same people, I guess) being employed elsewhere—maybe at a later time. This is a small harm in itself, but it is pretty much negligible in any case where job loss is actually under consideration. The two main cases where job loss might be bad are in cases of regulations, and in cases of technological advancement. To make you intuitively see that job loss is not worth thinking about in either case, let me give a representative example of each.

First, consider elevators. Back in the day, elevators were much harder to control than they are today. You had to accelerate the elevator with a lever, make sure it lined up with the floor, etc. Obviously not rocket science, but enough to warrant having elevator operators. Sadly for this profession, we soon invented automated push-button elevators, making operators obsolete. This was a huge mistake, due to the resulting job losses—and our workforce has never recovered since.

Not! Elevator operators losing their jobs is just about the least important thing that has ever happened. Even though elevators no longer having to be operated was only a small technological improvement, it would have been completely moronic to oppose it, just to keep people in their jobs. We might as well have paid people to dig holes and fill them again.

Second, consider asbestos. If you were not aware, we used to mine this fibrous silicate mineral and pack it into everything. This involved a whole infrastructure of mining, processing, manufacturing, and transporting the stuff across the globe. After a while, someone got the crazy idea that maybe, just maybe, inhaling clouds of microscopic needles that lodge in your lungs and give you mesothelioma decades later might not be a fantastic plan, and so we regulated it. This caused a large shift in the construction and manufacturing sectors, meaning many miners, factory workers, and installers lost their jobs.

Was this a bad thing to happen? I hope we can all agree that it was not. The job loss is essentially zero weight on the scale. It just doesn’t matter in the great scheme of things.

There are two different reasons why the job loss is not bad. First, the job loss is not permanent—it’s not of type (2) above. Second, whatever harm remains will often be outweighed by opposing reasons.
