item.title: Conceptual Analysis Is Stupid
item.description: Everything since Socrates was a mistake
item.dc:creator: Silas Abrahamsen
item.content:encoded:
Ever since Socrates went around annoying people on the street until it killed him, philosophers have been smitten by a certain method: Conceptual analysis. The central task of philosophy is to find the necessary and sufficient conditions of concepts like KNOWLEDGE, CAUSATION, and FREEDOM.1

This all peaked with the crown-jewel of analytic philosophy’s mythos: Edmund Gettier publishing the paper Is Justified True Belief Knowledge? which, as far as we know, is the only thing he ever did. Since then, much of philosophy has consisted in an eternal spiral of proposing definitions, and giving counterexamples, providing an infinite money and publication glitch for any professor lucky enough to catch the wave.2

Only, there is a small problem: This whole approach is bollocks! The idea of conceptual analysis is misguided—it was dead upon inception. I have talked about this several times before. I promise this is not a rehash of those old talking points. Rather I want to try to make a more systematic case for my position than I have before, as well as give you my alternative in conceptual engineering.

NB: This post has many images, so it doesn’t fit in an email. If you’re reading this in email, you have to open it in the app or browser to read the full thing.

What are concepts?

In good old analytic-philosophical fashion, let me start by saying what we’re even talking about. When I talk about concepts here, I’ll be meaning something like:

Units of semantic content.

This is suitably vague to not commit to any fancy ontology, as far as I can tell. Maybe they’re mental entities, or abstract objects, or whatever else people can dream up, but hopefully we can all agree on this much. And presumably they’ll figure in your thought somehow (we’ll get to that).

Let me spell it out a little more though. I don’t want to commit to any specific account of semantic content here, but it’s helpful to give some example accounts:

  1. Extensionalism: The content of a concept is its extension (the set of things it applies to). So the content of TIGER is all tigers.

  2. Intensionalism: The content of a concept is a function from possible worlds to extensions (or the set of possible things it applies to). So the content of TIGER is the set of all possible tigers.

  3. Hyperintensionalism: The content of a concept is something more fine-grained. E.g. a function from worlds considered actual and worlds considered counterfactual to extensions. So the content of TIGER might be… well something more complicated.3

More generally, I like the following sort of representation of what concepts are (inspired by ). Draw a space that has a dimension for every parameter that’s relevant to the content of concepts.

For instance, if what you take to be the relevant features of things are their color and number of sides, you might draw something like this:

Obviously this is a ridiculous example! You’d at least also have to include saturation! In fact, you’d probably want to include very many things, and hue and number of sides might not figure among them.4 But let’s roll with this for now.

The concept RED QUADRILATERAL would then be the following point:

You could of course also point to green triangles. From here, you might combine points, to create concepts like GREEN TRIANGLE OR RED QUADRILATERAL; and you might even draw areas, and so on. A concept can then be represented in this way.

For example, suppose you’re an extensionalist. You then take all actual things and map them onto the coordinate system, and then the content of RED QUADRILATERAL is all the things that intersect with the red quadrilateral-point.

Again, there should be a dimension for every relevant feature. So there might also be indexical dimensions (like how far something is from you), or any other random thing you can think of (like how it makes you feel).

The important thing is not whether this account is true in some “deep sense,” but just that it’s an adequate representation to help your thinking.

What is conceptual analysis?

Having made this representation, the next question to ask is: What can this tell us about conceptual analysis? Let’s first ask how we individuate concepts. In other words, what are the criteria for when a concept is the same concept? Here I suggest: By their shape in the parameter space.

I mean, I hope this should be uncontroversial. Concepts were supposed to be stuff with some sort of semantic content, and shapes on parameter space were supposed to represent this. So it stands to reason that concepts are individuated by this shape. At least that’s how they’ll be individuated, if you accept what I meant by “concept” in the beginning.

Okay, so in conceptual analysis what’s going on is that you’re trying to identify one concept with another. For instance, you have the concept KNOWLEDGE and you’re trying to label some region on parameter space with that. But what is this KNOWLEDGE you start with?

To give you my answer upfront, I don’t think there is any “deeper” fact about this. There are the shapes that correspond to JUSTIFIED TRUE BELIEF and to JUSTIFIED TRUE BELIEF ABSENT DEFEATERS etc. The question about which of these is KNOWLEDGE is empty. It’s a matter of labeling one of the shapes, and there’s no answer that’s truer than the other.

But you probably require a little more persuasion.

What are we aiming at?

In the dialogue Meno, the titular interlocutor presents the following paradox for conceptual analysis (not his words). Basically, either:

  1. You already know what the concept means, in which case there’s no need to analyze it. Or,

  2. You don’t already know what the concept means, in which case you wouldn’t be able to tell if some analysis is correct.

Socrates gives a bit of a non-solution, about recollecting things, which seems to move the bump in the rug around. But we can do better.

The psychological view

First, we might say that you already have a concept which you apply, but you don’t think about the rules of application—you just use them.

For instance, suppose you’re operating with the following concept:

What you “see” when you use it is not the above. Rather, you apply it to some cases. So you consider some things, and judge whether the concept applies, giving you a map like this:

You can then try to draw a shape to fit these, and if it turns out that there’s a counterexample (a dot on the wrong side of the line) that means your guess was wrong:

So what conceptual analysis is about is finding out what concepts you were already using all along.

This successfully evades the paradox: We take the first horn, but we have an explanation for why our already having the concept doesn’t mean that we already know the rules for application (i.e. the shape in our parameter space). Additionally, it operationalizes conceptual analysis nicely, giving clear truth-conditions.

Still, there are major problems.

1. Carrying the weight of our expectations

First, this account turns conceptual analysis into something of psychological self-investigation. All you’re doing is trying to figure out how your mind is operating. However, that makes it puzzling why it matters. Why does plotting out the shape of our own mental entities have such deep philosophical significance?

Furthermore, we have no reason to think that we’re talking about the same thing. The way I learned how to apply KNOWLEDGE was some mix of being given examples of how to use the word “knowledge,” as well as some intrinsic dispositions of concept formation and whatnot. But everyone will have had slightly different experiences and dispositions, so there’ll be differences in the concepts being used. And anecdotally, people often seem to have differing or unclear intuitions in various cases.

Simply put, on this account, saying that “KNOWLEDGE is X” is nothing other than saying that “as a matter of fact about my psychology, when I use the word ‘knowledge’ I mean to express a concept with the shape X.” Fine, but that’s hardly of much philosophical interest.

2. Being true

The bigger problem is that this account is false, which is about as big a problem as you can get. At least, it’s false as an account of why searching for necessary and sufficient conditions makes sense. When doing conceptual analysis we’re looking for necessary and sufficient conditions—for rules that univocally classify everything as being either an X or not an X. That is, the concepts we’re looking for are supposed to look something like this:

But that’s most likely not what the concepts we’re actually using look like. Rather they’ll look something more like this:

As said before, the way that we form concepts is probably something like extrapolating based on some core examples. But there’s no clear reason to think that we somehow form universal rules that apply cleanly to every possible case. For example, whether Mr. Truetemp (someone who reliably forms true beliefs about ambient temperature without knowing how) knows the ambient temperature. Upon hearing this for the first time, it’s unlikely that there’s a perfectly clear verdict—but if we were implementing sharp concepts, there should be.

For conceptual analysis to make sense, you’d have to think that the sharp picture is in some sense the “correct precisification” of the blurry picture. That is, the concept that we were really using all along. But:

  1. The psychological account doesn’t clearly license saying that the result of conceptual analysis can be an idealized version of the concept we’re using, rather than the one we’re actually using. And,

  2. It’s implausible to think that there is some single true sharp concept, that the blurry one is an approximation of.

I can’t say it much better than Wittgenstein does it in Philosophical Investigations:

76. If someone were to draw a sharp boundary I could not acknowledge it as the one that I too always wanted to draw, or had drawn in my mind. For I did not want to draw one at all. His concept can then be said to be not the same as mine, but akin to it. The kinship is that of two pictures, one of which consists of colour patches with vague contours, and the other of patches similarly shaped and distributed, but with clear contours. The kinship is just as undeniable as the difference.

77. And if we carry this comparison still further it is clear that the degree to which the sharp picture can resemble the blurred one depends on the latter's degree of vagueness. For imagine having to sketch a sharply defined picture 'corresponding' to a blurred one. In the latter there is a blurred red rectangle: for it you put down a sharply defined one. Of course—several such sharply defined rectangles can be drawn to correspond to the indefinite one.—But if the colours in the original merge without a hint of any outline won't it become a hopeless task to draw a sharp picture corresponding to the blurred one? Won't you then have to say: "Here I might just as well draw a circle or heart as a rectangle, for all the colours merge. Anything—and nothing—is right."

Additionally, conceptual analysis is looking for single, universally applicable concepts. But it’s not clear that my concept of KNOWLEDGE now is the same as the KNOWLEDGE I had when I was, say, 10 years old. In what sense can I then say that there is a single KNOWLEDGE to be found, which is more important than others?

The “further facts” view

To remedy this, we might instead try to go another route, and say that conceptual analysis is not aiming to find out what’s going on inside our own minds, but to find properties that are “out there.” KNOWLEDGE is not only a concept, but a property certain things have, and what we’re doing is trying to find out what that property consists in. If our concept is a blurry mess, then that’s on us. The property of knowledge is not blurry, and it’s our job to get our concept to align with this property.

This view easily escapes the two other objections. By making conceptual analysis about properties in the world, rather than about our own psychology, it’s much clearer why it’s worth caring about, and why it’s of philosophical interest. And we can say why it doesn’t matter that our own concepts are blurry: That’s a fault with us, but the property itself is perfectly crisp, and out there to find.

Predictably, I still have worries.

1. The psychological view is true

First, this view would seem to run right back into Meno’s paradox. If we already have a clear conception of the property in question, then what are we looking for? And if not, then how will we know we’ve got it when we find it?

By way of response, one might say that we don’t already know the concept, thus impaling ourselves on the second horn (where the psychological view went with the first). But we are not in the dark, as we can get evidence by considering hypotheticals. When I consider a Gettier case, I’m getting evidence that knowledge is not justified true belief, and so I’m refining my concept and getting closer to the truth, even though I didn’t know it to begin with.

The issue is that the first view we discussed is true. This might sound a little strange, seeing as I just argued that it’s not correct. And while it’s not correct as an account that can ground the legitimacy of conceptual analysis, it seems clearly right about what’s going on when we try to do conceptual analysis.

When I consider a Gettier case, what I’ll be making my judgement on the basis of is the blurry concept of KNOWLEDGE that I already have. I can’t make judgements on the basis of a concept I’m not using—that doesn’t make sense. For this story of how we learn about concepts to make sense, it seems we either have to tell some very mysterious story or some very spooky story about how we are not just reusing our old concepts—neither of which I expect will be particularly plausible.

There are of course some obvious ways in which we can make progress. Namely by rooting out inconsistencies, and trying to reach some sort of reflective equilibrium about how to draw the sharp concept. But here we’re back at the idealized psychology account before.

But as discussed, why think that there’s some correct way of precisifying our blob? And even if there is, why think that we have any good way of finding it? There’s no external “check” on whether we’ve taken the right path at any crossroads about how to make our judgements coherent. All we can do is cross our fingers and hope that we by some miracle end up in the correct place.

And, as mentioned earlier, it’s also not obvious that our concepts are the same, the same over time, or the same across culture. It’s hard to maintain that we could find the correct concepts with all this noise.

2. Why these concepts?

Second, this account still doesn’t explain why certain concepts are more “true” than others. In conceptual analysis, we try to find the concept of KNOWLEDGE. But we could also look for the concept of SCHMOLEDGE, which is like knowledge, except that it doesn’t apply before 1920.

We can say that it’s because we are looking for that property “knowledge.” But any instance of knowledge after 1920 will also have the property of schmoledge, so that only kicks the can down the road.

This points back to what I said about individuation. Both KNOWLEDGE and SCHMOLEDGE are simply shapes on our parameter space:

That’s all that characterizes them. What makes KNOWLEDGE KNOWLEDGE is that it has that shape, and likewise for SCHMOLEDGE. Why then is one more “correct”?

We could give a normative answer. We could say that SCHMOLEDGE is a horribly useless concept compared with KNOWLEDGE. I agree! It’s hard to imagine situations where we’d want to talk about SCHMOLEDGE rather than KNOWLEDGE. However, that’s not an explanation of why knowledge is the true concept, but an explanation of why it’s useful, and as we’ll see below, that’s something we can appeal to, even if we don’t accept conceptual analysis.

Instead we could say that KNOWLEDGE is important because it plays an indispensable role in our epistemological practices, or whatever. But we can construct a parody system, called shmepistemology. SCHMOLEDGE, SCHMELIEF, SCHMEVIDENCE, etc. play similarly indispensable roles in schmepistemology. Then the question becomes why epistemology is more correct than schmepistemology.

An obvious answer is to say that schmepistemology doesn’t give reasons in the same way that epistemology does. If schmepistemology tells me one thing, and epistemology tells me another, then I’ll side with epistemology, thank you very much. But notice that we’ve now given a normative explanation again, which is not enough to save conceptual analysis.

Instead we could say that what’s important is that KNOWLEDGE is the thing that we actually use. But that’s not particularly different from the psychological view, and what I said there applies here too: The fact that we, as a matter of fact, use some concept, does not justify taking that concept as being “privileged” or “truer” in any important sense.

We might similarly think that the traditional concept MARRIAGE implied a relation between a man and a woman. Recently, we have begun using the concept MARRIAGE*, which can also be between two people of the same sex. Was there something about the fact that MARRIAGE was the one we actually happened to use, that gave it any important claim to being more “true” than MARRIAGE*? Certainly not in any philosophically interesting way. Then why think that about KNOWLEDGE and SCHMOLEDGE?

3. It’s just weird

This is maybe not as much an objection as a sentiment I have, that you may or may not share. But I find that the idea that concepts latch on to certain properties in a way that goes beyond our own minds, and that we can discover, to be plain old weird. It flies in the face of what I take myself to be doing when applying concepts—at least when I reflect a little.

When I stipulate all the facts about a case, and then ask the question of whether this constitutes knowledge, I’m not attributing further properties, that were not already settled. Rather I’m classifying the case. That is, I’m judging how to group other—more specific—properties under broader labels.

Unreflectively, it might seem that I’m making substantive judgements, but that’s because I already come pre-packaged with certain classificatory schemes (like my learned concept of knowledge), that I’m employing. As we discussed earlier, these do not appear to me as explicit rules. Rather I’m applying the rules intuitively. This may make it look like I’m judging that there is some specific property that I’m figuring out whether or not is instantiated. But if I think about what’s going on, I cannot in good faith hold anything other than that I’m just applying labels.

Like, think back to the parameter space representation. How can we express that one shape is more “correct” than another, or “corresponds to some property” more? No concept could do that, as they’re groupings along these properties, rather than properties in their own right. The whole premise does not make much sense to me.

Conceptual engineering

It’s easy to tear down in philosophy. The real trick is building up, and unless I can give an attractive alternative, we have not gotten any further. Luckily, there is a great alternative: Rather than trying to figure out which concepts are correct, we can figure out which are best.

That is, instead of doing conceptual analysis, we should do conceptual engineering. For the reasons laid out above, it does not make sense to say that any concepts are better than others on descriptive grounds. Any shape in parameter space is just as “true” as any other—in fact, it’s almost a category error to say that there can be intrinsic descriptive privileging between concepts. But that does not mean that they’re equal in all respects: They differ in how good they are.

Some concepts are complicated and hard to use, some concepts serve as Schelling points for communication, some concepts lead us to overlook important distinctions, some concepts will implicitly classify certain people as wrong, etc. Concept choice is not neutral, but something that has effects in the world—and so we can submit it to normative scrutiny.

This gives us an easy way of “operationalizing” concept choice: Take some normative standard. Then take some concept choice, find out what will happen if we go with it, and then evaluate according to the normative standard. This gives an easy way of ranking concepts.5 The reason is that choosing what concepts to use is an action like any other.

I find this much more plausible than conceptual analysis. Any argument against this approach cannot appeal to any normative consideration, as that is already included in the engineering approach. You can’t say “oh well if we do that, then we’ll all be confused, no one will know what anything means, and we’ll end in carnage!” That’s an appeal to the negative normative consequences of following the approach,6 which the engineering approach will already agree with you about. It shows that we should generally use concepts that already resemble common concepts, or something like that.

To argue against this approach, you’ll have to give some account of the sense in which some concepts can be more correct than others. What is it that makes KNOWLEDGE correct and SCHMOLEDGE incorrect? And once you’ve done that, you would have to show how we could ever figure out what the correct concepts are, as well as why that standard is philosophically interesting in any way.

And even if you do that, you could never show that we should use that approach over the engineering approach. If we should, then it’ll already fall out of the engineering approach that we should, and so you’ll be agreeing with me.7

Conclusion

As I said, I think conceptual engineering wins comfortably. This is not because there’s some clean knockdown-argument—and if you were already inclined to conceptual analysis, you may not have been convinced. The problem for me is that analysis is a non-starter.

It’s easy to be introduced to something like the JTB analysis of KNOWLEDGE, and some Gettier cases, roll up your sleeves, and start doing the first-order theorizing. That is, conceptual analysis comes naturally to us, and we can proceed unreflectively engaging in it for large amounts of time, without considering what it amounts to. But as soon as we step back and examine what we’re doing, it’s hard to make sense of—as I hope I’ve shown.

I do not pretend that the options for making sense of conceptual analysis that I have presented are exhaustive. But I do think they are some popular options, and the problems with them are general enough to apply to many possible accounts.

To end this off, I’d like to invite the reader to reflect on the similarities between this dispute, and dispute around things like mereology, or natural kinds. If, like me, you have a skeptical disposition regarding the success of realist accounts in those kinds of domains, I hope you can see why that might apply here too. But I think the case against conceptual analysis (or lack of case for it) is stronger than in these other domains—even if you’re a realist there, you might be convinced against analysis.

As mentioned before, I have written about this issue a few times. The pushback I have gotten there has been limited, which is a shame. I know that many people—including, I believe, many of my readers—are fans of conceptual analysis. If you are one of these people, I’d be interested to hear how you respond to my case!
